studies.title: Glory To Him Who Journeyed
studies.meaning: The ayah opens not with the traveller but with a declaration that God is beyond limitation, and the journey follows as evidence of it. The one carried is called a servant, not a prophet or a messenger, which the commentators read as the highest title available. The stated purpose is not arrival but sight: to be shown signs. The two mosques are named and the ayah stops, leaving everything else to the reports.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical sources place the Night Journey late in the Meccan period, after the year in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) lost both his uncle Abu Talib and his wife Khadija and was driven out of Taif. The reports differ on the exact year and on whether the journey was in body or in vision; the commentators record the range. What they agree on is the setting: a community under boycott and ridicule.

keyTerms.note: A word of distancing rather than of praise. It declares that God is free of what is being implied, and here it precedes the journey, answering the objection before the claim is even made.
The verb already contains the night inside its root, so the added word for night reads as emphasis rather than as information. It marks a journey made under cover of darkness, brief and unannounced.

At the summit of the experience the Prophet is named by servitude alone. The commentators observe that the Quran reaches for this form at the highest moments, including the descent of revelation and the standing in prayer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel was ordinary in Arabia and often preferred. Caravans moved after sunset to spare the animals the heat, navigating by stars, and the road from Mecca to Jerusalem took about a month in each direction. That distance was the whole objection. Men in Mecca who had made the journey by camel asked the Prophet to describe the city, and the reports say he answered from what he had seen.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only surah in the Quran whose opening word is that declaration of God's transcendence. The phrase naming the Farthest Mosque occurs exactly once in the whole text, here and nowhere else. The surah carries two names in the classical sources, one taken from this opening and one from the Children of Israel, who dominate the ayat that follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The journey is attributed entirely to God: the verb is His, the blessing on the place is His, the showing is His. The Prophet is the grammatical object throughout, which keeps the event from becoming a feat of the traveller. The ayah then closes with two names, the Listener and the Beholder, both of them about perception. A passage concerned with being shown things ends by naming who does the seeing.

crossReferences.why: The Quran's other account of a granted vision, described at the lote tree of the utmost boundary.
Calls the sight God showed him a trial for the people, which is how Mecca received it.
Sets the two sanctuaries in one frame again, when the direction of prayer turned toward Mecca.

studies.applyIt: Notice the hour this ayah is set in. The journey came at the lowest point of the mission, not the highest, and it came without being asked for. If you are in a stretch where nothing is moving, try leaving tonight's quiet hours unfilled rather than drowning them in noise. Relief in this account arrives on its own schedule, in the dark, unannounced.

studies.title: Descendants Of Those We Carried
studies.meaning: The surah moves without transition from the journey by night to Moses and the Book given to him, placing this revelation in a line rather than at its start. The instruction quoted from that Book is a single negative: take no trustee besides God. Then the addressees are renamed. They are not simply a nation but the offspring of people rescued in an ark, and the man rescued with them is remembered for one quality, thankfulness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that turns almost immediately from the Night Journey to the history of the Children of Israel, which is why the classical sources also know it by their name. The Meccan audience had heard of Moses and Noah through Jewish and Christian communities in Arabia and through traders returning from Syria. Setting the new revelation alongside the old was an argument they could check rather than a claim they had to take on trust.

keyTerms.note: Not merely a helper. The word names the one you hand your affairs to and then stop managing yourself, which is why the sentence is framed as taking none besides God rather than as worshipping none.

The word carries lineage as an inheritance rather than as biology. Naming the audience by an ancestor's rescue makes the reminder personal: what they were told was told to people whose survival was itself a gift.
An intensive form. Not one who thanks but one whose thanking is constant and characteristic. The commentators attach it to reports of a man who gave thanks at every meal and every garment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the working memory of Arabia. A man could recite his fathers back many generations, and lineage decided who protected him, who owed him blood money, and whose feuds he inherited. To be addressed as the descendants of those carried in the ark was to be placed in a register the audience took entirely seriously. It named an obligation, not a curiosity about the past.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive word for the deeply thankful is applied to Noah exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah. Elsewhere the same form is used of God Himself, of a small number of the servants of David's house, and of the patient and grateful person in general. Its use for a named prophet here is unique.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together. Scripture is a chain, so the Book given to Moses and the one being recited in Mecca serve the same end, and the audience is not being offered a new religion. And gratitude is presented as a way of standing rather than a feeling: Noah is defined by it after surviving a flood that took everything, which places thankfulness on the far side of loss rather than in comfort.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly: thankfulness draws increase, and its refusal invites a severe reckoning.
Uses the same intensive form and observes how few of God's servants actually reach it.
Gives the rescue in the ark itself, the event this ayah calls the audience back to.

studies.applyIt: Take the phrase about the offspring of those who were carried and apply it to yourself once today. Name one person, two or three generations back, whose survival you depend on and never think about. A grandparent who crossed a border, or stayed when leaving was easier. Say their name aloud. Gratitude gets abstract fast when it has no one attached to it.

studies.title: A Decree Conveyed In Scripture
studies.meaning: A decree is announced in advance: the Children of Israel will spread corruption twice and will rise to great arrogance. Commentators read the verb as an announcement of what God knew would happen rather than as an order that they do it, and they note that the wording gives no dates and names no enemy. The ambiguity is deliberate. What is fixed is the pattern, twice repeated, and the link between overbearing height and what follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah addresses an audience that could see, in ruins and in the memory of older nations, what happens when a people entrusted with a scripture stops living by it. The classical commentators identify the two episodes with conquests of Jerusalem, most often the Babylonian and then the Roman, though they differ on the identification and some decline to fix it at all. None of them treat the ayah as a description of any living community.

keyTerms.note: The verb spans deciding and announcing, and the commentators divide over which sense is meant here. Read as announcing, it removes any suggestion that the corruption foretold was imposed rather than chosen.

The root covers spoiling and ruin of every kind, from tainted food to a broken social order. It is the standing Quranic opposite of setting things right, and it is never confined to private wrongdoing.
Height used against others rather than height as honour. The same root names Pharaoh's exaltation in the land, which makes the warning a familiar shape to the Quran's hearers rather than a new one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca sat on the trade road between Yemen and Syria, and merchants heading north reached the towns around Jerusalem. Ruined settlements lay along those routes, and Arabic poetry is full of the traveller halting at an abandoned camp to read what is left of it. A warning delivered in the shape of a nation's rise and ruin was not abstract to men who had ridden past the evidence and pitched their tents in it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places where the Quran gives a counted prophecy, two episodes rather than an open-ended warning, and it supplies neither dates nor names. The classical commentaries consequently set several identifications side by side and record their disagreement openly, which happens less often in narrative passages than in the ones dealing with practice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Foreknowledge and freedom are placed in one sentence without being reconciled. God announces what will happen; the people still do it, and are still answerable for it. The Quran lets the tension stand rather than dissolving it. The passage also refuses to turn a covenant into an immunity: having been given the Book is what makes the fall serious, not what prevents it.

crossReferences.why: Records an earlier refusal by the same people, when Moses called them to enter the land.
Lists the covenant terms taken from them in detail, and the breaking that followed.
Announces the same long consequence, others sent against them until the Day of Resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Notice how the warning is shaped. It is not aimed at strangers; it is aimed at the people who had the Book. If you have been given something you did not earn, an education, a faith, a family that told you the truth, ask once today what you have actually done with it. Advantage is described here as a heavier account, not a lighter one.

studies.title: When The First Promise Came
studies.meaning: The consequence arrives as a military event described in three strokes: servants belonging to God, possessed of great force, ranging through the houses. The commentators note that the invaders are called servants of God without being called righteous, which makes them instruments rather than models. Then the reversal. The turn is handed back, wealth and sons are restored, numbers grow. Ruin and recovery are both traced to one source, and neither is presented as permanent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is speaking to Mecca about a history it half knew, and the classical commentators differ over which conquests are meant, most often naming Babylonian and then Roman campaigns against Jerusalem. They agree on the shape rather than on the dates. Meccan hearers were being shown that a favoured community can be broken and afterwards restored, which was a warning aimed at them and not only a report about others.

keyTerms.note: A neutral title. Everything in creation serves God in this sense, so calling the invaders His servants describes their function within the event and says nothing at all about their standing before Him.
A verb of moving back and forth through a place, searching it thoroughly. It pictures soldiers between houses rather than an army outside the walls, which places the disaster inside the city.
The word names one sweep back in battle, the moment a retreating line wheels and charges. Applied to a whole people, it makes the recovery a single event rather than a slow improvement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a walled town the danger was never only the battle at the gate. It was afterwards, when soldiers went house to house: the granary emptied, the well fouled, the women and children taken. Arabia knew this from raids on its own settlements and from what traders reported of the Byzantine and Persian wars fought to its north. The picture in these two ayat needed no explaining to anyone who heard them.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage keeps switching person. The Children of Israel are named in the third person and then, without a pause, addressed directly as "you", a turn the classical rhetoricians treat as a recognised feature of Quranic style. Here it converts an ancient report into a direct summons, and the surah slides back out of it a few ayat later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves of the history are ascribed to God, which removes the comfort of reading defeat as His absence and victory as His approval. The invaders are instruments and are not endorsed. The restoration is a gift and is not a verdict. What the passage establishes is that outcomes are not a scoreboard of divine favour, and that a people's standing has to be read from its conduct rather than from its fortunes.

crossReferences.why: Says outright that such days are alternated between peoples, so that what is inside them is known.
Compresses the pattern into one line: a guilty town crushed, another people raised after it.
Gives the standing announcement behind these two episodes, and ends by naming God as forgiving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a bad stretch you came out of, and resist the two easy readings. It was not proof you were abandoned, and the recovery was not a certificate that you were right. Write one sentence about what actually changed in you between the two. That middle question is the one this passage asks, and the one we usually skip.

studies.title: Your Doing Returns To You
studies.meaning: A principle is dropped into the middle of a history: good done is done to your own account, and harm done is charged to it. The Quran states this in several places, but here it sits between two catastrophes, which changes its force. It is not a promise that virtue will be visibly repaid. It is an explanation of what the two ruins were. Then the second ruin is described, and the word used for the sanctuary is the word used for the two mosques in the surah's opening line.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was preaching in a city whose leading families measured a man by his fortunes, and this ayah cuts against that measure by placing the return of an action inside the actor rather than in his circumstances. Set within the account of Jerusalem's two ruins, it tells a Meccan audience that the same accounting reaches them, without naming them once.

keyTerms.note: The root means doing a thing beautifully, not merely correctly. It is the highest of the Quran's words for right action, covering excellence in a craft and in conduct alike, and the ayah repeats it twice in one breath.
The word names a place defined by an act rather than by a building, which is why it covers the sanctuary at Mecca, the one at Jerusalem, and any ground on which a person actually bows.
An intensive verb from a root meaning to smash into fragments. The Quran uses it of what became of earlier nations, and its choice here rules out reading the second ruin as a partial setback.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society kept careful accounts. Debts were remembered by name, blood money was reckoned in camels, and a merchant's word was his credit on a route he might not travel again for a year. The ayah borrows that habit of mind and turns it inward. The ledger it describes is one where the entry and the account belong to the same person, and no one else is able to settle it.
studies.didYouKnow: The second clause is unusually terse in the Arabic. Where the first says that doing good is for yourselves, the second drops the noun altogether and says only that doing harm is "for it", leaving the listener to supply the missing word. Grammarians have long noted the asymmetry, and read the compression as making the sentence turn faster than the mind can soften it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes moral consequence internal rather than transactional. Good is not exchanged for a reward; it is described as already belonging to whoever did it. That leaves divine justice intact without turning God into a paymaster. And by setting the principle inside a national history, the passage extends accountability from persons to peoples: communities, too, are said to receive back what they built.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle in almost identical words, and closes by denying any injustice in God.
Repeats it and adds the return, so the account is settled somewhere and not merely felt.
Reduces the idea to its smallest unit, an atom's weight of either kind, seen.

studies.applyIt: Pick one small thing you did well this week that nobody noticed, and one small thing you did badly that nobody caught. Hold them side by side for a minute without doing anything about either. This ayah says both are already lodged in the same place. Most of us keep a public ledger and a private one; it says there is only one.

studies.title: Perhaps Your Lord Will Show Mercy
studies.meaning: After two ruins the sentence opens with a particle of possibility rather than with a promise. Mercy is held out, and the condition attached is stated in three words: if you go back, We go back. The commentators read the second verb as answering the first exactly, so the door stands neither shut nor guaranteed. The passage then names the alternative without softening it. Hope and warning share one sentence, and neither cancels the other.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's opening survey of the Children of Israel before it turns to the Quran itself. The commentators observe that the ayah addresses the community just described, and that its wording leaves the future open rather than sealing a verdict on it. Heard in Mecca, where the Prophet's followers were a harassed minority, the same conditional reached the audience in the room: history had not finished with anyone.

keyTerms.note: A particle of hope. When the Quran uses it of God the commentators say the hope is well founded, since He is never uncertain, yet the form still withholds a guarantee the hearer might otherwise bank on.
The verb is repeated on both sides of the sentence, so the response is named with the same word as the act. Nothing new is threatened; what comes back is only what was there before.
The root yields both a woven mat and a wall that hems something in. Commentators take the second sense here, a place with no way out, while some hear the first as the image of a spread bedding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A besieged town in Arabia lived or died by whether the siege lifted. Terms could be offered and later withdrawn, and a tribe that broke its word once found the next negotiation much shorter. The conditional in this ayah works the way those settlements worked. Mercy was real and genuinely available, and everyone in the room understood that a second breach would be met exactly as the first was, without further discussion.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about going back is three words in the Arabic and uses the same verb twice, once of the people and once of God. This mirroring, where the divine response is named with the human verb, appears elsewhere in the Quran with the words for scheming and for forgetting, and the commentators treat every instance as correspondence rather than likeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah declines to dissolve mercy and justice into each other. It does not say God will forgive, and it does not say He will not. Hope rests on a particle that carries no obligation, which keeps a reader from both despair and presumption. The second half insists that consequence is not arbitrary: it answers conduct, in the same terms, and it can be restarted from either side.

crossReferences.why: Offers the same conditional to the Prophet's opponents: desist and the past is cancelled, persist and the pattern holds.
Puts the invitation at its widest, addressed to those who have wronged themselves most badly.
Returns to the same open future a little later, this time about the surah's own audience.

studies.applyIt: There is someone you have decided is finished, past changing. Maybe yourself. Notice that this ayah, spoken over two national catastrophes, still refuses to close the sentence. You do not have to trust the person again today. Just stop describing them, in your own head, as a settled case. Reopen the file. Leave it open until the evening.

studies.title: That Which Is Most Upright
studies.meaning: The claim is comparative rather than absolute. The Quran guides to that which is most upright, using a superlative built on the word for standing straight, so the promise is not that it points somewhere good but that it points to the straightest of the available ways. The commentators expand this to belief, conduct and the ordering of a community. Good news follows for those who act, and the reward is described only by size.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the surah that opens with the night journey. This ayah comes after a passage on the Children of Israel and two cycles of their rise and fall, so the claim about guidance is placed immediately after a history of what happens without it. The surah belongs to the late Meccan years, close to the migration. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A superlative from the verb to stand. It carries uprightness, correctness and stability at once, so the word describes a way that is both morally straight and structurally sound.
From the root for skin, because news that pleases shows in the face. The verb is for announcing something the hearer will be glad of, and its opposite is used elsewhere with heavy irony.
A plain word for large in size, not for noble or precious. The reward is left entirely undescribed except for its magnitude, which is a deliberate reticence the surah keeps up.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A road in Arabia was not a built thing. It was a remembered line between wells, and the difference between the straight route and a slightly wrong one was measured in days and sometimes in lives. Guides were hired for their memory of it. Calling a teaching the most upright way used a word every traveller understood in its ordinary sense before its moral one.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not name a destination. It says the Quran guides to that which is most upright and leaves the noun out entirely, so the phrase is grammatically incomplete and has to be filled in by the reader. Classical commentators supplied different nouns: the state, the way, the creed, the conduct. The omission is generally treated as deliberate breadth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran here describes its own function, and the description is modest in a specific way. It does not claim to be the destination; it claims to guide. That leaves the reader with work to do and explains why the ayah pairs guidance with those who act. The comparative form also concedes that other ways exist and are not simply nothing. What is asserted is that this one runs straightest, which is a claim open to being tested by living it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same book as healing and mercy, and as loss for the wrongdoers.
The request the Quran answers, spoken in every prayer: guide us to the straight path.
Opens the longest surah by naming the book as guidance for those who are mindful.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran today with a pencil and mark the single sentence that would change something if you took it seriously. Do not act on it yet. Just find it and underline it. The ayah says the book guides, which implies the reading is meant to leave you somewhere different from where you started.

studies.title: Asking For Harm As For Good
studies.meaning: Two ayat that look unconnected are set side by side. The first names what waits for those who deny the Hereafter; the second explains how they can. A person asks for harm with the same energy he brings to asking for good, because he cannot always tell them apart in advance. The closing clause gives the reason, and it is not malice but speed. Haste is described as constitutional, part of how the human being is made, which is why a request and a refusal can both be mercies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Opponents of the message were demanding that the promised punishment arrive at once, treating the delay as proof that nothing was coming. Several ayat from this period answer that demand, and this one answers it from inside the human being rather than from the argument. The commentators also read it more widely, of the curses a parent flings at a child in anger and would be horrified to have answered.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers calling out and calling upon, so one word carries an ordinary shout and a formal petition. Its use here treats a careless word as a genuine request, addressed to someone and heard.

The Quran's broad word for what damages, covering wrongdoing and misfortune together. Because it spans both, the ayah can describe a person asking for what will hurt him without accusing him of asking for anything wicked.
An intensive form naming a settled trait rather than a mood. The word occurs only here in the whole Quran, and it treats speed as a defect of judgement rather than of manners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society with no court of appeal, the spoken curse was a weapon. A wronged man would call down ruin on an enemy at the well or in the assembly, and poets built reputations on invective. Fathers cursed disobedient sons in the heat of an argument and went on living beside them. An audience used to words flung out at night and regretted by morning knew what this passage was describing.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive word for haste here appears nowhere else in the Quran. A related statement elsewhere goes further and says the human being was created of haste, using a construction that makes the trait sound like a material rather than a habit. Reciters also note that the verb for calling in this ayah is written without its final long vowel, an old spelling preserved in the standard text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places a limit inside the person rather than outside him. He is not refused because God withholds, but because he asked badly and did not know it. That turns unanswered prayer into a form of protection rather than a silence needing explanation. It also undercuts the demand for immediate proof that runs through this surah: a creature who cannot judge his own requests is a poor judge of God's timing.

crossReferences.why: States the same trait as a fact of creation, then tells the hearer not to rush God.
Gives the general principle: you may hate what is good for you and love what harms you.
Sets the answering of prayer inside nearness, which is what makes a careless request dangerous.

studies.applyIt: Think back to something you prayed hard for and did not get. Not to feel better about it, but to check the arithmetic: would you still ask for it now, knowing what came instead. Then take one thing you are pressing for this week and set a reminder six months out to look at it again. Haste is much easier to see in the past tense.

studies.title: Two Signs, One Erased
studies.meaning: Night and day are called two signs, and then one of them is described as having been wiped. The commentators read the erasure as the removal of light, so the night's sign is legible precisely by being dark, while the day's is made revealing so that work becomes possible. Three purposes follow in order: earning, counting the years, and reckoning. The ayah closes by saying everything has been set out in detail, which is a claim about the text as much as about the sky.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just finished arguing about the Hereafter and turns to the sky, which was the shared evidence in a dispute where scripture was not shared. Mecca's calendar, its pilgrimage season and its trading year all ran on lunar observation, so the ayah appeals to something its audience managed professionally. No specific occasion is reported; the commentators read it inside the surah's run of signs.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of wiping writing off a surface. It makes the night a page that has been cleared rather than one never written on, which is why darkness counts here as a sign and not an absence.
Grammatically the day's sign is called seeing rather than seen. The commentators explain this as the cause standing in for the effect: daylight does not look at anything, it makes looking possible.
The same root yields the counting of days and the accounting of deeds. Placing it beside the number of years lets one word carry both the almanac and the final audit without the ayah saying so.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan year was read off the sky. The new crescent opened a month, the sacred months set when caravans could travel unmolested and when the fairs opened, and debts fell due at the turn of a season rather than on a numbered date. Men who moved goods between Yemen and Syria carried their schedules in their heads by moons. Losing the count was not an inconvenience; it dislocated the whole year.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the Quran uses here for a sign is the same word it uses for a verse of the Quran itself. So the ayah is saying, quite literally, that night and day are two verses, one of which has been erased. That double sense runs through this surah, which repeatedly calls both the sky and the recitation by one name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats absence as informative. Night is not the failure of a sign but a sign made by subtraction, which is a small argument with long reach: what is withheld can communicate as much as what is given. The purposes then listed move from the practical to the moral without a seam, so that earning a living and knowing the reckoning belong to one ordered world rather than to two.

crossReferences.why: Assigns the same two purposes, the number of years and the calculation, to the sun and moon.
Names the same pair as a mercy, one half for rest and one for seeking bounty.
Says the alternation itself is for whoever wants to reflect or to give thanks.

studies.applyIt: Tomorrow, do one thing at the hour it was made for. If you have been working at midnight and sleeping through the morning, move a single task, the one needing your clearest head, into the first two hours of daylight. At the end of the week check whether it cost you anything. The ayah divides the day into two kinds of time; most of us have stopped.

studies.title: Read Your Own Book
studies.meaning: An image from Arabian augury is taken up and turned around. The bird a man released to read his fortune is replaced by a record fastened to his own neck, so that what he took for luck is described as his doing, and it travels with him. On the Day of Resurrection it is produced already open, and he is told to read it himself. The second ayah then removes every intermediary: no witness, no advocate, no accuser. He is handed the evidence and asked to do the arithmetic.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Before Islam, Arabs consulted birds ahead of a journey or a raid, startling them and reading the direction of flight as a good or ill omen, and the word this ayah uses for a person's fate comes straight out of that practice. The Quran keeps the word and empties it. The commentators read the passage as answering an audience that treated outcomes as fortune, and that was arguing at the time that resurrection could not happen at all.

keyTerms.note: The word means a bird, and by long usage the omen taken from one. Fastening it to the neck moves fate from the sky to the body, so that nothing about a life stays external to the person living it.
Used of a scroll unfurled for reading. The detail carries weight because a sealed record could be disputed; one opened in the owner's own hands cannot be, and the ayah gives no room to argue with it.
From the root of counting. Telling a person he is sufficient as his own reckoner does not make him the judge; it says the evidence needs nobody else to read it aloud on his behalf.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before a caravan set out, someone would flush a bird and watch where it went. To the right meant one thing, to the left another, and a raid could be called off on the strength of it. Written records existed but were rare and costly, kept on parchment or hide by the few who could read. To hand a man a scroll about himself and tell him to read it was an image with real weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a person's fate is the ordinary Arabic word for a bird, carried over from divining by flight. The Quran uses the same root elsewhere when opponents tell a prophet that they take him for a bad omen, and each time it turns the word back on the speakers. Here the omen is fastened, physically, to the neck.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage relocates judgement. It is not that God will discover something about the person; it is that the person will finally see what was attached to him all along. That makes the Day a disclosure rather than an investigation. And by removing every intermediary at the decisive moment, it undercuts each arrangement, tribal, ancestral or bought, by which somebody else might answer in your place.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same record produced, and the dismay of finding nothing small left out of it.
Gives the other side of the scene, a man calling people over to read his book.
Says the writing covers not only deeds but the traces those deeds left behind.

studies.applyIt: Try the second half literally tonight. Take five minutes and write down what you actually did today, not what you meant to do, in the flat voice of a record: woke, said, spent, ignored. Do not grade any of it. The ayah does not ask you for a verdict; it asks you to look at the page. Most of us have never once read a day back.

studies.title: No Soul Carries Another's Load
studies.meaning: Three statements, each tightening the one before. Guidance and straying are first described as landing on whoever chose them, rather than as services rendered to God. Then the load is made non-transferable: no bearer carries another's burden, in either direction. Then a limit appears on God's own practice, that no punishment comes before a messenger has. The commentators discuss at length what reaches a person who never heard, and they record more than one view without settling it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah arguing about accountability with people who expected ancestors, idols or chiefs to answer on their behalf. The closing clause was also heard against a Meccan complaint that the message was new and its consequences unfair. No single occasion is well attested for the ayah, and the commentators place it inside the surah's running argument about who actually owns a deed.

keyTerms.note: An active participle with no noun attached, so the Arabic says only "no bearer bears". Leaving the subject unnamed makes the rule cover everyone without the ayah having to list anybody.
From a root for the heavy pack strapped on for a journey. The Quran treats wrongdoing as weight rather than as stain, which is why it can be spoken of as carried, set down, or added to.
One sent with something to deliver, as distinct from a sage who reasons his way to the truth alone. The choice of word makes the condition external: the argument has to have reached you from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loads were the daily arithmetic of caravan life. A camel took what it could take, and the two sides of a pack had to balance or the whole thing shifted on the road. Men hired themselves out to carry, and a debt could be assumed by a kinsman about as easily as a pack could be moved onto a stronger back. That transfer, ordinary in every other part of life, is what the ayah refuses.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul bearing another's burden appears five times in the Quran, in five different surahs, each time inside a different argument. It is among the most repeated single sentences in the text. In one of those places it is followed immediately by a scene in which someone weighed down calls for help with the load and nothing is lifted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established. Responsibility is personal in a way that no relationship dissolves, which rules out inherited guilt and inherited credit together. And divine justice is described as bound by its own announced practice: God says He does not punish before sending. That is a striking sentence, because it makes the sending of messengers a condition God has held Himself to rather than a favour He might have withheld.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause and then dramatises it, with a weighed-down soul calling for help unanswered.
States the other half, that a messenger was raised in every community without any exception.
Gives the principle from the far end: no town ruined while its people were unaware.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are carrying somebody else's load, and where you are trying to hand off your own. A parent's disappointment you have made into your fault. A decision of yours you keep explaining by the people around you. Pick one of the two today and say the true sentence out loud, once, to nobody: that one is mine, or that one is not.

studies.title: When The Affluent Break Bounds
studies.meaning: The mechanism of a town's ruin is laid out in a single sentence whose grammar has always been difficult. God commands its comfortable class, they break bounds, the sentence falls due, the place is levelled. Commentators differ over what is commanded: obedience, which is then refused, or an ordering of events in which ease is allowed to run its course. None of them read it as a command to sin. The next ayah widens out, counts the generations since Noah, and rests on God's knowledge of what His servants do.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The message was resisted hardest by the men with most to lose, and the Quran says so repeatedly in this period, putting the affluent of a town at the head of every refusal. The surah addresses an audience whose caravans passed settlements now standing empty. The commentators read these two ayat inside that argument rather than tying them to a particular occasion, none of which is well attested here.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being made soft by ease. The word is not simply rich: it names people whose comfort has taken away their capacity for hardship, and the Quran nearly always sets them at the front of a refusal.
The root pictures a date slipping out of its skin. It describes stepping outside a limit rather than breaking one named rule, which is why translators reach for wide words like transgression.
Used across the Quran for a decision already spoken and now falling due. Saying that the word became justified against the town makes its ruin the maturing of something said, not a sudden verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's wealth sat with a handful of families who financed the caravans, held the offices of the sanctuary, and lent at interest to everyone else. They had the most to lose from a message that unsettled the pilgrimage trade. A poor man in Mecca risked a beating for following the Prophet; a merchant risked his creditors, his partners and his name. These ayat describe a pattern their first hearers were standing inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the comfort-softened occurs in only a handful of places in the Quran, and in nearly all of them the same people are the ones who refuse. Twice the text says outright that no warner was ever sent to a town without its affluent declaring they rejected what he brought. The pattern is offered as a historical regularity rather than as a complaint about money.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ruin is presented as a process with steps rather than a bolt out of the sky: comfort, refusal, a sentence maturing, then collapse. That keeps human choice intact in the middle of a passage about divine destruction. The closing line then changes the ground of the argument. After all the history, the case rests on God's knowledge of what His servants actually did, offered as sufficient without further demonstration.

crossReferences.why: States the regularity outright: no warner reached a town without its affluent rejecting him.
Gives their reasoning, that they found their fathers on a road and are following it.
Points at the empty houses of towns ruined for turning unappreciative of their own livelihood.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where comfort has quietly become an argument in your life. Something you have stopped questioning because questioning it would be expensive. It need not be money; it can be a routine, a job, a friendship you have outgrown. Name it once today and decide nothing. The warning here is not about having much. It is about no longer being able to hear.

studies.title: Whoever Desires The Hastened Life
studies.meaning: The ayah does not deny that the world can be got. It says the opposite: it will be given, and quickly, but on terms the recipient does not set. Two conditions are stacked onto the giving, what We decide and to whom We desire, so the grant is made and then twice qualified. Only after that does the outcome arrive, and the two words closing the ayah describe standing rather than sensation: condemned, and driven off.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community around the Prophet was poor and watching its opponents prosper, and this passage answers the obvious question about that. The commentators read it as addressing intention rather than possession: what is described is a person whose whole aim stops inside this life. No particular occasion is well attested, and the surah sets the ayah at the head of a short comparison between two kinds of effort.

keyTerms.note: Literally the thing hurried forward. Naming this world by its speed rather than by its substance ties the ayah back to the description of the human being as hasty a few ayat earlier.
A passive participle from the root of censure. The word concerns reputation rather than pain, so the first thing named about the outcome is how the person now stands in everyone's estimation.
From a verb for shoving something off and away. Paired with blame, it makes exclusion the second half of the loss: not merely judged badly, but removed from the presence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was close to the worst thing that could happen to an Arab. A man cut off from his tribe had no protection, no price on his blood, and nobody to answer for him at a well or on a road. The poets wrote about outcasts as the walking dead. The two words closing this ayah put a person in exactly that position, and the audience felt them socially before they felt them theologically.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's usual name for this world means the nearer or the lower one. Here it is swapped for a word meaning the hastened, which carries that sense in only three places in the whole text. The two closing words are also a rare pair: each appears a handful of times, but this is the only ayah that puts them together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates provision from approval. Receiving what you wanted is described as a real grant from God and as no evidence whatever about your standing, which dismantles prosperity as a spiritual measure in both directions. It also makes intention the hinge. Nothing here says the world was taken wrongly. What is judged is that it turned out to be the whole of what was wanted.

crossReferences.why: Sets the two harvests side by side, and says one leaves no share in the other.
Repeats the grant in this life, paid in full and with nothing withheld from it.
Gives the other half of the comparison, then says God's gifts are not restricted.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you would still be doing this week if nobody ever found out you had done it. Not as a test to pass, just as a measurement. The ayah is not against getting things; it is about where an effort comes to rest. One honest answer, kept entirely to yourself, tells you more about your aim than a month of intending better.

studies.title: Effort That Is Appreciated
studies.meaning: The counterweight to the ayah before it arrives with three conditions rather than one. Wanting the Hereafter is not enough. There has to be effort, effort of the right kind, and belief underneath it. Then the return is named not as payment but as appreciation, which is a warmer word than the argument requires. The next ayah refuses the obvious conclusion: God's giving in this world reaches both parties, and the passage ends by saying that giving is fenced off from nobody.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The believers were a poor and pressured minority watching men who mocked the message do well in trade, and these two ayat address that discrepancy without evading it. The commentators read the pair as a single argument: worldly provision cannot be the measure, because it is handed out to both sides at once. No particular occasion is well attested, and the sequence itself supplies the setting.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical exertion, used of walking briskly and of working for a living. Its choice keeps pursuit of the Hereafter from collapsing into an inner state, since the word first of all means moving.

A passive participle of thanking, so the effort is described as received with gratitude rather than as paid for. It places God in the position of the one who acknowledges, which is unusual phrasing anywhere.
From a root for an enclosure built to keep animals in or out. Saying the gift is not fenced makes openness the default state, and any restriction the exception that would need explaining.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A working day in Mecca meant physical effort: loading, driving, hauling water, walking a valley road under sun. The word this ayah uses for striving was ordinary vocabulary for exactly that, and the same root names the hurrying between two hills that pilgrims still perform. When the Quran asked for effort toward the Hereafter, it reached for the language of labour rather than the language of feeling.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for appreciated effort appears twice within the first twenty ayat of this surah. Earlier it describes Noah as a deeply thankful servant, and here it describes human effort as received with thanks. The direction of gratitude reverses between the two, which is a striking thing for one root to do inside one page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims that people usually separate are held together here. Ultimate outcomes depend on aim and effort; immediate provision does not. Insisting on both at once removes the two commonest misreadings of prosperity in a single stroke, that wealth signals favour and that poverty signals virtue. The closing clause then makes openness a property of God's giving rather than a policy, stated as a fact and not as a promise.

crossReferences.why: Says a person attains only what he strove for, using the same word for striving.
Names the two harvests, and adds that one of them leaves no share in the other.
Gives the first half of this comparison in full, the world paid without any shortfall.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you want for the next life and ask what you actually did about it this week, in the sense this ayah uses: moving, spending time, going somewhere. Not intending. If the honest answer is nothing, pick the smallest physical version of it and do that today. The word here describes effort somebody could watch from across a room.

studies.title: Greater In Ranks And Favours
studies.meaning: The reader is told to look at visible inequality rather than to explain it away. Some are favoured over others, plainly, and the ayah does not soften it. Then the comparison moves: whatever the differences here, the differences there are larger, in rank and in preference both. The next ayah opens the surah's long run of counsels, and its subject is not conduct but attachment, since setting up a second god is where a divided aim begins.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah now begins a sequence of counsels that classical commentators treat as one unit, bracketed at both ends by the same words about setting up another god beside God. The first bracket falls here. Mecca's sanctuary held images belonging to many tribes, and what was being asked was not the addition of a deity but the removal of every other one, which cost more socially than it sounds.

keyTerms.note: A verb of giving something extra rather than of judging worth. It makes visible inequality a distribution and not a verdict, which is why the ayah can point at it without either defending or condemning it.
From the root for a stair. The plural describes the next life as graded rather than split in two, leaving room for degrees of difference that this life's blunt categories cannot register at all.
From a verb for abandoning someone mid-fight when they were counting on you. The word names exactly the failure a second god would turn out to be: help that is absent at the moment it is needed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Kaaba was a shared sanctuary. Tribes kept images there, pilgrims came from across the peninsula, and the honour and the income of Mecca's leading houses rested on that arrangement. Asking a man to set aside one god among many was not asking him to change an opinion. It touched his alliances, his trade, his family's standing in the assembly, and his safety on the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The prohibition against setting up another god appears twice in this surah, in wording that differs only by a connecting particle, opening and closing the run of counsels between them. The classical commentators treat the repetition as a frame, so everything in between about parents, wealth, speech and honest dealing is held inside one question about attachment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes inequality real and non-final at the same time. It is not denied, explained away, or justified; it is set beside a larger scale on which the present ordering weighs almost nothing. That is a claim about proportion rather than about compensation. And by moving straight into the first counsel, the surah suggests the practical danger of visible inequality is not envy so much as divided loyalty.

crossReferences.why: Says the ranks in this world are themselves the test, set inside the same distribution.
Explains the unequal allocation as what lets people need one another and work together.
Closes the frame with the identical sentence, at the far end of these counsels.

studies.applyIt: Pick the person whose situation you have been comparing yourself against, upward or downward, and try one day without doing it. When the comparison starts, let it finish and do not act on it. The ayah does not tell you the gap is imaginary. It tells you the scale you are using is the small one, and that the ranking you can see is not the ranking that lasts.

studies.title: The Wing Of Humility
studies.meaning: The command to worship God alone and the command to treat parents well are joined in one decree, which the commentators note is a joining repeated across the Quran. Then the instruction narrows to a single scene: old age, in your house, one parent or both. Three things are forbidden, and the first is the smallest, a sound of irritation. The passage ends by handing the reader a prayer, since the debt named in it cannot be paid.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage of commands that runs through much of the surah, sometimes compared to a set of foundational instructions because of how it is arranged. The commentators report no specific occasion. In Mecca, accepting the message often set a young person against their own household, so a passage insisting on tenderness towards parents arrived where it was hardest to hear and most needed.

keyTerms.note: Not a word but a sound, the noise made through the teeth at something tiresome. Forbidding it sets the floor extremely low, since anything worse is already covered by the two prohibitions that follow.
A bird lowering its wing over its young, joined to a word for being humbled. The image asks not for obedience but for a posture, and the passage adds that it must come out of mercy.

From the root behind the word for Lord, which also means to nurture something to completion. The prayer uses the parents' nurturing as the ground for asking God's, which is a careful and deliberate echo.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no institutions for the old. A parent who could no longer travel, trade or fight lived in a son's house and depended on it entirely, and the household's other work went on around them. Failing eyesight, deafness and slowness were dealt with by family or not at all. The scene the ayah describes, both parents ageing under your roof, was the ordinary end of a life rather than an unusual burden.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word forbidden here is a single syllable that is not really a word at all, a sound rather than a term. Commentators have long observed that the passage works by degrees: forbid the smallest sign of impatience and every larger form is settled without being listed. The clause about old age also uses a construction meaning whether one or both, leaving no gap.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing parents immediately after the exclusive worship of God gives the relationship a weight nothing else in human life receives. It is not made equal to worship; it is made the first thing after it. The passage also refuses to treat gratitude as sufficient. It ends in a prayer, because what the child owes exceeds what the child can return, and asking God to supply the difference is the only honest response the ayah offers.

crossReferences.why: Adds the mother's carrying and weaning, and sets a limit where obedience would mean association.
Gives a prayer at forty that thanks God for the favour shown to one's parents.
Commands kindness to parents while refusing them on the one matter that cannot be conceded.

studies.applyIt: If your parents are alive, call one of them today and let them finish a story you have heard before. Do not correct a date. If they are gone, say the prayer at the end of this passage once, by name. The ayah gives it in the past tense, as something they already did, and it works either way.

studies.title: The Right Of The Relative
studies.meaning: The passage turns from outward duty to what sits inside a person, which the commentators read as covering the moments when someone does the right thing without feeling it. God is said to know that, and forgiveness is attached to a particular description: those who keep turning back. Then the frame widens outward again, to the relative, the poor and the traveller, each named as holding a claim rather than receiving a favour. The warning that follows is not about giving too much but about spending with no direction at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the run of counsels that follows the passage about parents, and read by the commentators as its completion: the outward duty is stated first and then the state of mind behind it. Mecca had wealth and a widening gap between its families, and travellers arrived constantly for trade and pilgrimage with no claim on any local household. This wording gives them one.

keyTerms.note: The word belongs to the vocabulary of entitlement, used of debts and legal claims. Calling what the relative receives a right rather than a gift moves the giver from benefactor to someone settling an account.
Literally the son of the road. The idiom describes a person whose only present relation is to the route he is on, which is exactly why he has no family nearby to fall back upon.
From the root for scattering seed. The image is of flinging out what should have been planted, which is why the word treats waste as misdirection rather than as generosity carried too far.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality was Arabia's welfare system and its loudest boast at the same time. A traveller arriving at nightfall was fed, and poets built whole reputations on how many camels a man slaughtered for guests. The boasting was the problem: display could consume in one evening what a household needed for a season. Naming the poor and the traveller as holders of a claim moved the act from reputation to obligation.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind squandering occurs in only two ayat in the entire Quran, and they are these two consecutive ones. It arrives three times across them: as a verb, as the verbal noun that intensifies it, and as a name for the people who do it. Because it follows immediately after an instruction to give, the warning about waste cannot be read as an argument for holding on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things stand together here. God's knowledge reaches into intention, so an account is not settled by conduct alone. And wealth is described as carrying claims that did not originate with its owner, which reframes giving as transfer rather than as kindness. The description of those who keep turning back matters too: forgiveness is attached to a repeated motion rather than a single act, so what is being praised is direction, not record.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same recipients inside its definition of righteousness, before it mentions any ritual.
Describes the balanced spender who neither wastes nor withholds, naming a middle between two extremes.
Names these categories again, with the reason wealth should not circulate among the rich alone.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose claim on you you have been treating as a favour you generously grant. A cousin you help now and then. A neighbour. Try doing the same thing once this week while thinking of it as settling rather than as giving. Nothing changes on the outside. Almost everything changes on the inside, and that inside is what the first ayah says God knows.

studies.title: Neither Chained Nor Flung Open
studies.meaning: The first ayah covers the case nobody plans for: you have nothing to give and somebody is asking. What is asked of you then is not an apology but a particular quality of speech, easy and unhumiliating. The second gives the shape of spending as two failed postures of a single hand. Chained to the neck is one failure; flung fully open is the other, leaving a man sitting there with nothing. The image is physical, and the middle is left unspecified on purpose.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) would sometimes have nothing at all to give a petitioner and would turn away rather than speak, and they read the first ayah as addressing exactly that discomfort. Some sources tie it to particular askers among the Meccans; the reports vary, and the wording itself is general enough to reach anyone with empty hands.

keyTerms.note: From the root of ease and of what comes lightly. The word asks for speech that costs the hearer nothing, so that a refusal is not allowed to become a second injury laid on top of the first.
The word for a hand fastened to the neck by an iron collar, which is the posture of a prisoner. Applying it to stinginess makes the withholder the one who is bound, rather than the one holding on.
Used of a beast driven until it can go no further. It names the state of the over-giving man precisely: not condemned, but finished, with nothing left for anybody who comes next.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's hand was his reputation. Arabic verse praised the open-handed and mocked the tight-fisted in lines that circulated for generations, and a chief who fed his tribe through a hard season was remembered for it. There was a real danger on the other side too. Households were ruined by competitive giving at feasts, and the sight of a once-generous man reduced to asking needed no explaining to anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah closes with a construction this surah returns to four times: a person left sitting or thrown down, described by two paired participles. The other three concern setting up another god and desiring the fleeting life. Placing over-spending in that company is startling, and it is the surah's own way of marking the two failures as symmetrical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Generosity is described as a virtue with two edges rather than a quantity to maximise, which is unusual, since most moral vocabulary treats giving as good without limit. Here the man who empties himself is named alongside the man who holds everything back, and both are pictured immobilised. What the passage protects is the capacity to keep giving, and that requires something to remain. The first ayah then makes speech itself a form of provision when nothing else is left.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two extremes and calls the middle between them a settled quality of character.
Says a kind word and forgiveness are better than a gift followed by injury.
Sets out the claims this pair is balancing: the relative, the poor and the traveller.

studies.applyIt: The next time you cannot help someone who asks, do the harder half of this passage. Do not go quiet, do not over-explain, and do not promise something just to end the conversation. Say one short, warm, honest sentence and let that be enough. The ayah treats the words you use when your hands are empty as a real thing you are handing over.

studies.title: He Expands And He Restricts
studies.meaning: An ayah about provision is set immediately before two of the surah's hardest counsels, and the order is the argument. God is said to widen and to narrow what people receive, and to be watching them closely while He does it. Then the first counsel addresses a fear that was costing children their lives in Arabia, and answers it by naming who actually feeds them. The second draws its line around approaching rather than around the act, which the commentators note is the wider boundary of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some tribes in Arabia buried infant daughters, and the sources give both destitution and fear of dishonour as reasons; the Quran returns to the practice several times in this period and treats it with unusual directness. The surah is speaking to a trading city where a household's fortunes rose and fell with the caravans, so the fear named here was not imaginary. No single occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The verb for opening a hand or unrolling a cloth. The same word appears a few lines earlier of a human hand spread too wide, so one image serves for God's giving and for ours at very different scales.

Not poverty in general but the point at which supplies are exhausted. Naming that precise fear rather than an abstraction shows the ayah answering a calculation somebody had actually sat down and made.
The Quran's word for a wrong whose ugliness belongs to its definition, used of acts that damage more than the people directly involved. It carries the sense of something that exceeds every bound.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan lost to raiders, one bad season, a debt called in, and a Meccan household could go from comfortable to desperate inside a year. Daughters could not be sent out with the caravans, and their marriages cost the family. The arithmetic that led some fathers toward the practice named here was cold and, on its own terms, coherent. The ayah answers the arithmetic itself, by relocating who is doing the providing.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions the killing of infants in several places, and in one of them the buried child is described as being questioned on the Day of Judgement about the crime for which she was killed. The accusation is put to the victim rather than to the killer, and the text leaves the question standing there unanswered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is made a matter of divine distribution, and then a conclusion is drawn from it: because you do not control the supply, you are not entitled to act as though the arithmetic were yours to solve. The second counsel establishes something different again. Some harms are guarded against at a distance, because the danger is treated as beginning with proximity rather than with the act, and the household these ayat protect is fragile in both directions.

crossReferences.why: Describes the father's face darkening at the news, and the choice he then sits weighing.
Puts the question to the buried child herself, and leaves it standing there unanswered.
Gathers the same counsels into one address, opening at parents and closing on a straight path.

studies.applyIt: Notice where a fear about money is quietly making a decision for you. Not a large one; something small, this week. Something you are not doing, or someone you are not helping, because the arithmetic looks tight. Look at that arithmetic honestly and then separate how much of it is knowledge from how much is forecast. This passage puts a great deal of weight on that difference.

studies.title: A Soul Made Sacred
studies.meaning: Life is described as having been made inviolable, and the exception is named in one phrase rather than spelled out, which the commentators read as pointing to lawful process rather than to private judgement. Then the ayah turns to the family of someone killed unjustly and gives them standing. And having given it, it immediately limits it. The restraint clause is the heart of the passage: authority is granted and bounded in the same sentence, and the closing words promise support to the one who stays inside the bound.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabia ran on the blood feud, and its logic was collective. A killing obliged a whole kin group to answer, and the answer often exceeded the injury, which is how feuds ran for generations over an original death nobody could remember clearly. The surah addresses that world. The commentators read the passage as recognising the family's standing while cutting away the escalation that made the system unliveable.

keyTerms.note: The same root gives the sanctuary at Mecca its name and the sacred months their protection. Using it of a human life places a person in the category of things that may not be violated, whoever they are.
A word for backing that can be produced and shown, used elsewhere of proof and of a ruler's power. It gives the family a recognised standing rather than permission to act on their own reading.
The verb for overstepping a proper measure, the same one used of wasting wealth. Applying it here treats vengeance as a quantity that can overrun its limit exactly as spending can.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before Islam, a strong tribe might answer one of its men killed by taking several from the other side, and boast about the ratio in verse. Weaker groups absorbed losses they could not answer, which entrenched the imbalance. Whole alliances formed around old killings. When this ayah gives standing to the victim's family and then bars excess in the same breath, it is addressing the actual machinery of Arabian violence.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause forbidding the killing of a soul God has made sacred, except by right, appears three times in the Quran in almost the same words: once in a Meccan list of what the Lord has forbidden, once here, and once in a description of the servants of the Most Merciful. Each time it sits inside a run of paired counsels rather than standing alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does two things at once that are usually pulled apart. It refuses to treat a wrongful killing as a private matter to be absorbed, giving the injured family real standing. And it refuses to let that standing become unlimited, because the restraint is placed inside the very sentence that grants the authority. What is protected is not one party but the ratio, so that redress does not become the seed of the next injury.

crossReferences.why: Sets one life against all of humanity, in both directions, taken and saved.
Lists the same inviolability among the marks of the servants of the Merciful.
Keeps the right to answer an injury while calling restraint and pardon the higher course.

studies.applyIt: Think of a wrong done to you that you were right about. The clause worth sitting with is not the one granting standing; it is the one that follows. Ask what proportion would actually look like here, and whether what you want is that or something larger. You can be owed something and still overshoot. This ayah treats those as two separate questions.

studies.title: Full Measure And True Scales
studies.meaning: Three matters are joined that look unrelated until you notice what they share. An orphan's property, a pledge given, and a measure poured out are all things nobody else is checking. The orphan is too young to audit his guardian, a pledge lives in the memory of two people, and a merchant's scale can be adjusted by a thumb. The passage sets a standard for exactly those situations, and calls the pledge itself something that will be asked about, as though it were a person waiting to give evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca lived by trade, and its standing depended on the reliability of its merchants along a route where nobody could verify a transaction after the caravan left. Orphans were common in a society where men died on the road or in raids, and their property passed to a guardian with no supervision. The commentators read these ayat inside the surah's run of counsels rather than tying them to any single reported occasion.

keyTerms.note: From a root for firmness and strength. The word marks a stage rather than a birthday, so the standard being described is the young person's actual capacity to handle what is his, not a number.

A word for a precision balance which the early philologists generally treated as borrowed from outside Arabic. It occurs only twice in the Quran, in this ayah and in one other, both times about weighing honestly.
A passive participle. The pledge itself, not the person, is what the Arabic makes the subject of questioning, which the commentators read as making the promise something that stands up and testifies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grain, dates and oil were sold by volume and metal by weight, and every market had disputes about both. A merchant kept his own measures, and a slightly generous scoop for buying and a slightly mean one for selling could go unnoticed for years. Meanwhile a guardian holding an orphan's camels had no ledger to answer to, and the child would not be able to ask for a decade.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a precise balance appears only twice in the whole Quran, here and in a passage set in the mouth of an earlier prophet warning his own trading town. Early Arabic philologists generally regarded it as a loanword taken into Arabic from outside, which is unusual for a term the text uses in a moral instruction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates integrity where verification fails. What links a child's inheritance, a private promise and a market scale is that in each the wrongdoer is safe from discovery, and the standard is set precisely there. That makes honesty a relation to God rather than a response to being watched. The closing phrase raises the stakes further: what is best is also described as arriving at the best outcome, so integrity is presented as accurate rather than merely noble.

crossReferences.why: Names the defrauders who take full measure for themselves and short others, in three lines.
Sets the human scale beside the balance God raised with the sky itself.
Treats the orphan's coming of age in detail, and the handing over of the property.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where nobody is checking you. Hours you bill, an expense you round, something you agreed to that the other person has half forgotten. Pick the smallest one and correct it today, quietly, without telling anyone you did. This passage puts three unwatched things in a row on purpose. The point is not the size of the correction; it is that you noticed the category.

studies.title: What You Do Not Know
studies.meaning: A short prohibition with a wide reach. The verb forbids following the track of something, as a hunter follows a trail, so what is ruled out is pursuing a claim you cannot verify. The commentators list what it covers: saying you saw or heard what you did not, giving an opinion without grounds, repeating a rumour, and testifying beyond your knowledge. Then the three faculties are named and each is said to be answerable.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a run of commands in the middle of the surah that moves from worship of God alone to parents, relatives, spending, killing, orphans, weights and measures, and then to this. The classical sources report no specific occasion. In a society whose news, law and lineage were carried entirely by report, the reliability of what people said was the load-bearing structure of ordinary life.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning the back of the neck, and so to come up behind something and track it. The image is of a person walking after a claim rather than examining it.

A different word from the usual one for heart, closer to the seat of understanding and burning attention. Naming it alongside hearing and sight makes the inner judgement a sense organ like the others.
A passive participle of questioning. The grammar leaves it open whether the faculties are asked about, or asked, and the commentators record both readings without settling between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in that world was written down twice. A debt, a marriage, a genealogy, a boundary between grazing grounds all rested on what men remembered and were willing to state. Poets could ruin a family with a line, and a rumour about a woman could end a household. Testimony was the only record there was, which is why a prohibition on speaking past your knowledge was closer to civil engineering than to etiquette.
studies.didYouKnow: The three faculties are listed in the order hearing, sight, heart, and that order recurs throughout the Quran without variation. Hearing comes first, which is the reverse of how English usually ranks the senses. Commentators connect the sequence to how a child develops and to how revelation arrives, since a message is heard before it is seen or understood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accountability is extended to the equipment rather than only to the act. That is a strong claim: it means the intake of information is itself a moral matter, and that a person is answerable for what they let in and what they let past. It also implies the faculties are on loan. Something you will be questioned about is not simply yours, which quietly reframes curiosity, attention and belief as things held in trust.

crossReferences.why: Instructs verification when news arrives from a source that may not be reliable.
Names the same problem earlier in the chain, at suspicion and the search for faults.
Describes hearing, sight and skin testifying against their owner on the Day.

studies.applyIt: Before you forward or repeat one thing today, stop and ask where you got it. Not whether it sounds true, but the actual source. If you cannot name it in one sentence, let it go unshared. Most of what passes through a person in a day fails that test, and noticing how much is the point of the exercise.

studies.title: Neither Piercing Nor Towering
studies.meaning: The prohibition is answered with two physical facts instead of a moral argument. Do not walk in exultation, because you cannot bore through the earth and you cannot reach the height of the mountains. The commentators note that the reply addresses the strut itself, the way a proud man carries his body, rather than the inner state. The second ayah then gathers the whole list of commands and says its evil is hateful to your Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the sequence of commands that began with worship of God alone. Status in Mecca was performed in public: the walk to the sanctuary, the seat at the assembly, the retinue behind a man of standing. The leading opponents of the message were also the leading families, and their bearing in the streets was part of the argument they were making. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: Not pride as an inner attitude but the visible pleasure of showing off, a bounce in the step. It is the word for a horse that is fresh and skittish, and it names a manner rather than a belief.
A verb for tearing cloth or splitting something open. Applied to the earth it is deliberately absurd, and the absurdity is the argument: the strut implies a claim the walker's own body disproves.

A passive participle from the root for aversion. Applied to God it is understood as describing what He does not approve, and the classical commentators are careful to keep it from implying a change in Him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a small town where everyone could see everyone walk. Cloaks that trailed in the dust were a display of wealth, since only a man with servants could afford to ruin cloth. Processions to the sanctuary were staged, and a chief moved through the market at a particular pace. The two comparisons the ayah chooses, the ground and the mountains, were the two fixed things any Meccan could see from anywhere in the valley.
studies.didYouKnow: The same prohibition appears again later in the Quran, in the advice a father gives his son, where it is paired with an instruction not to turn your cheek away from people. Both times the correction is physical: a walk, a face. The Quran addresses arrogance more often through posture than through belief, which is easier to notice in yourself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pride is treated as a factual error before it is treated as a sin. The argument offered is about size and capacity, which places the human being accurately in the world rather than condemning him in it. That is a gentler and more durable correction than shame. The second ayah then attaches a divine response to the entire list of commands, so ordinary conduct is not morally neutral territory that God notices only occasionally.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same command and adds a measure for the voice and the stride.
Describes the servants of the Merciful by how they walk: gently, and answering peace.
Shows the whole trajectory of exultation in wealth, ending with the ground opening.

studies.applyIt: Watch how you walk into a room today, once. Not to correct it, just to see it: the pace, where your eyes go, whether you look at the person who is already there. Most of what other people read from you happens before you speak. The ayah picks the walk because it is the part of the self you notice least.

studies.title: Some Of The Wisdom Revealed
studies.meaning: The run of counsels is closed by naming what it was: some of the wisdom your Lord revealed to you. Not all of it, and not a code, but a portion. Then the same sentence that opened the sequence returns word for word, so the whole passage about parents, wealth, speech, life and honest dealing is bracketed by a single question about attachment. The ending differs from the opening only in what follows the warning, which is heavier here than it was there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan.
