These counsels were given to a community with no state, no courts of its own and very little power, which is worth noticing: they were offered as wisdom to be lived rather than as a system to be enforced. The commentators treat the bracket as deliberate. Mecca's objection was never to good conduct, which its own tribes prized, but to the exclusive claim that stands at both ends of the passage.

keyTerms.note: The root carries the sense of a bridle: what restrains and steers. Wisdom in this vocabulary is not accumulated information but the capacity to place a thing correctly, which is why counsels can be called by the name.
A verb for communicating quickly and privately, used of a hint or a signal as well as of revelation. It describes transmission that is direct and unobserved rather than a text handed over in public.

From a verb for pushing something off. The same word closes an earlier ayah in this surah about a life aimed only at the immediate, which links the two failures by their outcome rather than their content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wisdom literature was familiar in Arabia. Proverbs, maxims and the sayings of famous judges circulated by memory, and a man known for sound judgement was consulted across tribal lines. What was strange in this passage was not its advice, much of which any elder would have endorsed, but its attribution. These were not the accumulated conclusions of experience. They were being described as sent.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for wisdom occurs exactly once in this surah, and it occurs here, applied backwards to the counsels just given rather than forwards to anything new. Nothing in that run is called law or command; it is named as wisdom disclosed. The classical commentators note that the label covers the whole passage, not only the ayah it sits in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By calling the preceding counsels a portion of wisdom, the ayah refuses to present them as exhaustive, which leaves the moral life larger than any list. And by closing the frame where it opened, it makes ethics dependent on attachment rather than the reverse. The order matters: the passage does not argue that right conduct leads to right belief. It presents the whole run of counsels as what a single loyalty looks like when it is lived out.

crossReferences.why: Opens the same frame in identical words, at the other end of these counsels.
Calls wisdom an abundant good, given to whomever God wills, and rarely grasped.
Gives another run of counsels bracketed the same way, from a father to his son.

studies.applyIt: Read the ayat between the two brackets in one sitting, without stopping to study them. Parents, relatives, the poor, the traveller, speech, spending, children, honesty, the scale. Notice that they arrive as a list and not as a system, and that they are described as a portion of something larger. Then pick the one you skipped over fastest, and sit with that one instead.

studies.title: Sons For You, Daughters For Him
studies.meaning: The argument is made by holding two Meccan beliefs together until they collide. The same men who considered a daughter a misfortune assigned daughters to God, and called the angels female. The ayah does not attack the low view of daughters directly; it uses it, asking whether God has kept for Himself what they would not want. The verdict is delivered in a single phrase about the size of the statement. The following ayah observes that the argument has been turned every way, and that turning it only increases the recoil.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Several Arabian tribes regarded certain angels as daughters of God, and the Quran returns to this claim repeatedly in the Meccan period, each time pressing the same inconsistency. The same society is described elsewhere as receiving the birth of a daughter with shame. The commentators read these ayat within the surah's argument about the Quran's reception rather than tying them to a single reported occasion.

keyTerms.gloss: has He then chosen for you
keyTerms.note: The verb means to select the pure part of a thing, the way cream is skimmed. It sharpens the question: are you saying He kept the residue for Himself and skimmed the best off for you.
A verb for rotating something so it can be seen from every side, also used of shifting winds. It describes the Quran restating one case in many forms rather than repeating itself.
The word used of a camel shying and running from something that startles it. It makes the reaction physical and involuntary rather than a considered reply to the argument being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sons carried the tribal name, fought, inherited and defended the well. Daughters married outward, and their marriages moved property and honour into another house. A man's standing in the assembly was counted partly in sons. That arithmetic was so ordinary it went unspoken, which is what makes the ayah's manoeuvre effective: it does not have to explain the preference, only to point at where it had been quietly applied.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran raises this same inconsistency in at least four separate Meccan surahs, each time by contrast rather than by direct denial, and one of those places asks the question in almost the same words as this one. The strategy is consistent: the claim is dismantled by the objectors' own valuation instead of by an argument they would have to accept first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attacks a way of thinking rather than a doctrine. Attributing offspring to God projects human continuation onto Him, and the ayah exposes the projection by showing that the projectors did not even project their own best. It also establishes something about revelation in the line that follows: clarity is not what produces acceptance. The same turning of the argument that opens one hearer is described as driving another further off.

crossReferences.why: Sets the attribution beside the father's darkened face at the news of a daughter.
Ties the naming of angels as female to disbelief in the Hereafter specifically.
Asks whether they witnessed the angels' creation, and says the claim will be recorded.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself, once today, doing what this ayah exposes: holding two standards without noticing. What you accept in yourself and refuse in someone else, or what you demand of a stranger and excuse in a friend. Do not fix it and do not feel bad about it. Just find one, and say what it is. The argument here works by making people see their own arithmetic written down.

studies.title: They Would Have Sought A Way
studies.meaning: The argument is short and turns on a single consequence. If other gods existed alongside Him, they would have looked for a route to the Throne, because power that is real does not sit quietly beside a greater power. Commentators read the seeking in two ways: as rivalry, or as the lesser gods themselves seeking nearness to the true one. Either reading leaves the Meccan position incoherent, since their gods neither contended nor drew near. The second ayah answers not with a further argument but with a declaration of distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Meccans did not deny God; they held that lesser powers had a share, and approached them for intercession and for local needs. The Quran's Meccan arguments therefore aim less at the existence of God than at the coherence of a hierarchy with junior partners. The commentators place this ayah in that debate, and no specific occasion is attested for it beyond the standing dispute at the sanctuary.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for a road. Its plainness is the point: the ayah does not describe a metaphysical relation but a path someone would take, which is what any genuine power would look for.

The image names sovereignty rather than furniture, and the classical commentators are careful to say so, treating it as the seat of authority over creation without describing anything a person could picture.

keyTerms.gloss: and He is exalted far above
keyTerms.note: From the root of height, and the same root the surah used earlier of an arrogance that rises against others. Here the height is God's, which is the one place the word carries no fault at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca understood power as hierarchy. Tribes had chiefs, alliances had senior and junior partners, and everyone knew that a strong client eventually pressed against his patron. Nobody in that world believed two forces could hold real power in one place indefinitely without one testing the other. The ayah puts its case in terms the assembly used every week about their own arrangements.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran makes this argument from the incoherence of divided power at least three times, in three different Meccan surahs, and each version turns on a different consequence: seeking a way to the Throne, the ruin of the heavens and the earth, and each god carrying off what it had made. The conclusion is the same; no two of them run the same route to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues for oneness from the nature of power rather than from scripture or authority, which makes it usable by anyone who accepts that real power does not stay passive. It also shows the Quran's characteristic move at the close: an argument is followed not by a summary but by a declaration of transcendence, so that the conclusion is worship rather than proof. What has been demonstrated logically is then removed from the reach of comparison.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same argument to a different end, the ruin of both heavens and earth.
Adds the third version, each god taking away what it created and overpowering the rest.
Continues the surah's concern with how God is named and how He is addressed.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the argument ends in praise, not in a scoreboard. Try that shape once today. When you finish thinking something through, whether it is a problem at work or a question you have been circling for weeks, do not stop at the conclusion. Add one sentence that is not an argument at all. The surah models a mind that reasons and then stops reasoning on purpose.

studies.title: A Praise You Cannot Hear
studies.meaning: Two ayat that seem unrelated and are not. The first says the seven heavens, the earth and everyone in them declare God's exaltedness, and then widens further: there is nothing at all that does not do so, though you do not grasp how. The second describes a curtain placed between the reciter and those who reject the hereafter. Read together, the universe is speaking and the barrier is on the listener's side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah answering objections about other gods and about resurrection. The passage that follows describes coverings over the hearts of those who turn away and heaviness in their ears. Classical reports connect this section to opponents who would gather to listen to recitation at night and then mock it, though the details vary. The surah belongs to the years just before the migration.

keyTerms.note: The root means to swim or travel swiftly through something. The verb is not praise in general but the act of removing every unworthy thing from God, which is why a stone can do it by simply being what it is.
A verb for grasping the inner sense of something rather than merely hearing it. The ayah does not say the praise is inaudible; it says the failure is in the comprehension.
A name for the one who does not act on provocation at once. Placed at the end of an ayah about universal praise, it explains why those who withhold it are not immediately dealt with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sound carried a long way in the valleys around Mecca, and people were used to hearing things they could not place: wind through a gorge, a caravan bell before the caravan, the noise of a well being worked at night. A claim that everything was making a sound nobody could interpret was not strange to that audience. What was strange was being told the fault lay in their hearing.
studies.didYouKnow: The barrier in the second ayah is described with two words that both concern covering, one a curtain and the other meaning hidden, so it is a veil that is itself veiled. Commentators note that a barrier nobody can see is worse than one they can, because the person behind it does not know it is there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first ayah makes worship the default condition of existence rather than a human speciality. Everything that exists already declares what God is by being what it is; the human being is the one creature that can decline. That reframes belief as joining something already in progress rather than starting it. The second ayah then locates unbelief in perception rather than in evidence, which is why the surah answers it with forbearance rather than with proof.

crossReferences.why: Birds in flight are said to know their own prayer and their own manner of praising.
Everything in the heavens and the earth prostrates, willingly or unwillingly, with its shadow.
Says the same recitation is healing for some and deafness for others.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and stand still for one minute without your phone. Do not try to feel anything. Just list, silently, five things in front of you that were not made by a person. The ayah says each of them is already doing something you cannot hear. One minute is enough to notice how rarely you stop long enough to check.

studies.title: Veils Over Understanding
studies.meaning: The barrier named in the previous ayah is now described from the inside: coverings laid over the hearts so comprehension does not land, and a weight in the ears. Commentators read this as the settled result of long refusal rather than an arbitrary sealing, since the Quran elsewhere shows the same people turning away first. The last clause is the sharpest detail. What triggers the recoil is not a command or a threat but the mention of the Lord by Himself, with no other name beside Him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years of the mission when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) recited publicly and the leading families had settled into refusal. The commentators attach no single occasion to it. They place it in a running description of how the recitation was received in Mecca: some listened closely and left unmoved, and the naming of one Lord without the tribal deities was the point at which an audience broke up.

keyTerms.note: A plural of a word used for the sheath that protects something stored. It does not say the heart is destroyed. It says something has been laid over it, so the organ is intact and the reception is not.
The root covers both a heavy load and hardness of hearing, and Arabic keeps the two senses together. Sound still arrives; it lands on something weighted down and does not carry any further.
Used of animals that shy and scatter at a sudden noise. The image is reflex rather than considered rejection: the body moves before the argument has been weighed, which is what the ayah describes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan sanctuary held images belonging to many clans, and a family's standing was bound up with the god it kept and the pilgrims that god drew. To hear the Lord named alone was to hear the whole arrangement set aside, including the fees, the guardianship and the alliances built on them. The recoil this ayah describes had an address and an account behind it, not only a belief.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for coverings over the heart appears four times in the Quran, always paired with a heaviness in the ears. Three of those are statements God makes about people who refuse. The fourth is placed in their own mouths, where they announce it about themselves as a kind of boast. The description and the boast use nearly the same words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Read alongside the rest of the Quran, the covering is described as coming after refusal rather than before it, which keeps responsibility with the person while admitting that habits of refusal harden into something the person no longer steers. The passage also locates unbelief in a faculty rather than in an argument. Nothing here says the objectors lacked evidence. It says they had stopped being able to take it in.

crossReferences.why: Places the same image of screened hearts and blocked ears in the objectors' own mouths, as a declaration.
Describes listeners who attend closely to the recitation and still carry nothing away from it.
States the sealing of hearing and hearts after describing people already settled in refusal.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next piece of advice that bounces off you before you have weighed it. Not the ones you consider and reject, the ones you are already moving away from as they arrive. Name one. You do not have to accept it today. Just sit with the fact that you turned before you looked, and consider why that one.

studies.title: A Man Bewitched
studies.meaning: Two things are reported at once: that opponents came and listened closely to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and that they withdrew to settle privately on what to call him. The charge they reach is not that he lies but that he is under a spell, which concedes that something unusual is happening in the recitation while denying its source. The opening clause is the weight of the ayah. God knows the purpose behind the listening, not merely the fact of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources describe leading opponents slipping out at night to hear the recitation, meeting one another on the way home, agreeing not to return, and returning anyway. Reports of that kind circulate widely enough that the commentators treat the general picture as sound while differing over the particulars. The ayah sits in a stretch of the surah concerned with how the message was received rather than with argument.

keyTerms.note: A noun for confidential talk, used here as though the men have themselves become the whispering. Arabic can put people in the place of the abstract noun for emphasis, so secrecy reads as their condition, not their activity.

A passive form: someone worked upon, not someone working magic. The accusation therefore files him among victims rather than deceivers, which is part of why it could be said aloud without quite calling him dishonest.

The form carries deliberate effort rather than passive hearing. It is the verb for straining to catch something, so the ayah grants the opponents real attention before reporting what they did with it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on reputation, and a charge that could be repeated in a market was worth more than one that had to be proved. Poets and soothsayers were familiar figures, and a man said to be touched by unseen forces was handled with a mixture of caution and dismissal. Calling him bewitched let the objectors account for the force of what they had just heard while granting it no authority over them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for bewitched occurs three times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah. Here it is the Meccan objection to the Prophet; later in the same surah Pharaoh says it of Moses in almost the same phrasing. The third instance repeats the Meccan charge inside a list of other things the objectors demanded instead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine knowledge is made specific here rather than general. The ayah does not say that God knows everything and so knows this; it says He knows what the listening was for, which is the one thing the listeners could keep from each other. The passage also shows a pattern the Quran returns to. Rejection rarely denies that revelation has force. It relocates the force to a source that costs the hearer nothing to accept.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same accusation in Pharaoh's mouth against Moses, later in this same surah.
Repeats the charge beside the objectors' demands for a treasure or a garden of his own.
Shows a verdict on the recitation being reached deliberately, by a man who weighed it first.

studies.applyIt: When you disagree with something, try naming the reason out loud before you name the person. The objectors here had heard something they could not answer, so they described the speaker instead. That move is available to everyone and it feels like an argument while it is happening. Catch yourself at it once this week, then go back to what was actually said.

studies.title: Rocks Or Iron
studies.meaning: The comparisons the objectors had coined are dismissed in one line, and their real difficulty is then quoted: bones and scattered fragments cannot become a person again. The answer does not argue the point. It raises the stakes instead, telling them to be the hardest thing they can imagine, stone or iron, and leaving the promise untouched. Commentators read the reply as a refusal to trade in degrees of difficulty, since nothing is harder for God than anything else.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the stretch where the surah records the labels being tried out against the message: poet, soothsayer, bewitched man. Resurrection was the single teaching that Meccan society found least credible, and the objection is quoted in these words repeatedly across the Meccan surahs. The commentators describe no particular occasion here, only the standing argument that ran in the assemblies of the city.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a parable or a coined similitude. It suggests the labels were crafted rather than blurted, worked over between opponents until they found one that would carry in conversation.
Not simply dust. The word means something broken down until the pieces no longer show what they came from, which is why it is paired with bones as the last recognisable stage before that.

The hardest worked material the audience knew, imported and expensive in western Arabia. Naming it after stone climbs a scale the listeners themselves used for durability, then abandons the scale as irrelevant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in Arabia was shallow and quick, and the desert returns a body to bone within a season. People had opened old graves when digging or when moving a settlement, and had seen exactly what the objection describes. Iron came north from Yemen or by sea and was worked into blades and tools that outlasted their owners by generations. The two materials in the reply were the most permanent things anyone present had handled.
studies.didYouKnow: The objection quoted here appears a second time in this same surah, word for word, near its close. The first time it is put in the objectors' mouths as a live question; the second time it is recited back to them as the reason for their outcome. The surah quotes them accurately and then hands the sentence back unchanged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply reframes what the disagreement is about. The objectors are treating creation as a process with a difficulty curve, where remaking scattered matter would be harder than assembling it once. The answer denies that the curve exists, which is a claim about the kind of power involved rather than about its quantity. What follows in the next ayah completes the argument by pointing back to the first origination, an event the objectors already accept.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this objection in identical wording later in the surah, there as the ground of a verdict.
Answers the same question about decayed bones by pointing to the one who first produced them.
Narrows the point to fingertips, promising restoration down to the smallest ridges of a hand.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have decided is beyond repair: a habit, a relationship, a piece of yourself you have written off. Notice that the verdict rests on a comparison you made, not on a measurement. You do not have to feel hopeful about it today. Just hold the verdict a little more loosely for one week and see whether anything moves.

studies.title: Who Will Bring Us Back
studies.meaning: The dare of the previous line runs on to its limit, any created thing the audience thinks harder still, and then the conversation is predicted rather than reported. They will ask who could bring them back, and the answer sends them to a fact they already hold: the one who shaped them the first time. Their second question is about timing, and it is answered without a date. Commentators note that the reply concedes nothing and promises nothing except nearness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that stages the standing dispute over resurrection as a live exchange. The commentators do not attach a particular occasion to it. They read it as the summary of many conversations in the city, where the argument moved predictably from denial of possibility to a demand for a date, once the possibility could not be closed off.

keyTerms.gloss: originated you, split you into being
keyTerms.note: The root carries the sense of splitting something open so that what is inside appears. It is used of first origination rather than repetition, which is why it settles the question the objectors are raising.
A precise verb for jerking the head up and back, the gesture of open mockery. It occurs only here in the whole Quran, and it records the body language of the argument rather than its content.

A particle of expectation, not of certainty about timing. Used here it withholds the date the questioners wanted while leaving the event unqualified, so the answer is neither a refusal nor a calendar.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan assemblies argued in public and in the open, in the shade beside the sanctuary or at the edge of the market, and a gesture carried as far as a sentence. Shaking the head backwards with the chin raised was a recognised way of declining without speaking, the sort of thing a senior man could do across a circle. The ayah records the gesture because everyone present would have seen it used.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the mocking head shake in this ayah occurs exactly once in the entire Quran. The Quran often reports what objectors said; recording how their heads moved while they said it is rarer, and here the physical detail arrives before the words it accompanies, so the reader sees the gesture and then hears the question it belonged to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument turns on consistency rather than on power. Whoever grants a first origination has already granted everything the second requires, so the burden is moved back onto the objectors' own position. The unanswered question about timing then does a second kind of work. Knowledge of the hour is withheld from everyone, including the one delivering the message, which keeps the promise from becoming a prediction anybody could test and discard.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that repeating the creation is easier for God, the principle assumed in this reply.
Answers the same demand for a date by placing that knowledge entirely with God alone.
Keeps the same posture of nearness without measurement: the hour may well be close.

studies.applyIt: There is probably a question you keep asking that has a known answer you do not like, and a second question about timing that nobody can answer. Try separating them on paper tonight. Put what you actually know in one column and what you are only waiting on in the other. Most of the weight usually turns out to sit in the second column.

studies.title: Say What Is Best
studies.meaning: The first ayah closes an argument about resurrection: on the day you are called, you will answer with praise, and the whole span of your life will look brief. Then the register changes completely. Servants are told to say the thing that is best, and a reason is given that is not about manners: Satan provokes friction between them. The commentators read the sequence as connecting the shortness of life to the pointlessness of quarrels.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage before it records opponents asking who would restore them once they were bones and dust. This one answers and then turns to the community itself. Classical reports connect the instruction about speech to friction between believers and those who abused them in Mecca, where an answer in kind would have cost more than it gained. The details of the reports differ.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a sudden goad or prick, the kind that starts a fight rather than sustains one. It suggests the first push rather than the argument, which is why the instruction addresses the opening sentence.
A superlative with the noun left out, so the phrase means the best of whatever is available to say. It does not ask for something acceptable; it asks for the top of the range each time.

A verb of remaining somewhere temporarily, used of a traveller stopping at a place. Applied to a whole life it frames the years as a halt on a journey, which is what makes the estimate come out short.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Words started wars in Arabia. A satirical verse against a clan could not be answered except by blood or by a better verse, and feuds lasting decades were traced back to a single insult at a well or a market. Reconciliation was the work of respected men who travelled between camps. In that setting, telling believers to say the best available thing was a strategy for survival as much as a virtue.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction is not given directly. God tells the recipient to tell My servants, so the command reaches its audience through a messenger and is framed by an expression of belonging. Commentators note that the same phrase, My servants, is used in the Quran at moments of particular tenderness, including the ayah about never despairing of God's mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A quarrel between believers is given a cause outside both parties. That is not an excuse, since the instruction still falls on the speaker, but it changes the diagnosis: the friction is being worked at from somewhere, so the first harsh sentence is the point of entry rather than the whole problem. Placing this immediately after a scene of resurrection also sets the scale. The dispute will look, from there, like part of a very short stay.

crossReferences.why: Push back with what is better, and an enemy may become a close friend.
Describes seeking refuge with God at the first prompting from Satan.
The same estimate on the Day: they whisper that they stayed only ten days, or one.

studies.applyIt: Pick the person you most often speak sharply to, and give yourself one rule for today: no first sentence that you would not want repeated back to you. Only the first sentence. That is where this ayah locates the problem, and it is small enough to actually hold for a day.

studies.title: Your Lord Knows You Best
studies.meaning: Three moves are made in one short ayah. The knowledge of the audience is placed with God rather than with anyone arguing about them; mercy and punishment are both left open, and mercy is named first; and the messenger is told the outcome is not his to secure. Commentators read the last clause as relief rather than reprimand. He carries the delivery and not the result, and the second half of the sentence is what makes the first half bearable.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a community under pressure and to a messenger watching people he knew refuse the message. The commentators place it among the ayat that repeatedly limit the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to conveying rather than compelling, a theme running through the Meccan surahs before permission to fight was ever given. No single occasion is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: A comparative form used absolutely, so it means better than anyone else rather than better than one rival. Placed at the head of the ayah, it removes the question of who these people really are from human hands.
The word for someone appointed to act on another's behalf and answer for the outcome, as in commerce. Denying the role denies accountability for results, not responsibility for the message.
The conditional is repeated twice in the same form, once before mercy and once before punishment, so neither is presented as the default. The grammar keeps both possibilities genuinely open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An agent in Meccan trade held real authority. A merchant travelling to Syria would appoint one to sell on his behalf, settle prices and answer for losses when the accounts were read out. Everyone in the audience had either been such an agent or hired one, and knew that the burden of a bad season fell on the man who had accepted the appointment. Telling the messenger he held no such appointment lifted a specific and familiar weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an entrusted agent appears across the Quran in two very different roles. In most places it describes God, whom believers are told to rely on entirely. In a handful of places, including this one, it is denied of the Prophet. The same term marks the one who can carry outcomes and the one who cannot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By naming mercy before punishment while granting both the same conditional form, the ayah keeps hope ahead without turning it into an assurance. The wider point concerns the shape of prophecy itself. A messenger who cannot guarantee results also cannot be blamed for them, which protects the message from becoming a contest of persuasion, and protects the messenger from measuring his faithfulness by how many people agreed.

crossReferences.why: States that guidance is not the Prophet's to give, however much he may want it for someone.
Uses the same limit in different words: a reminder is what you are, not a controller.
Denies the same role of appointed agent in a passage about those who turn away.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person you have been quietly trying to change. Write down what part of that is actually yours: what you say, how you treat them, whether you stay in the room. Then write down the part that is not: whether they change. Keep doing the first list this week and let the second one go for now.

studies.title: No Power To Relieve
studies.meaning: Two claims are set side by side. God knows every creature in the heavens and the earth, and He has ranked some prophets above others, giving David a scripture of his own. Then the objectors are told to go ahead and call whatever they invoke, because the test is simple: those objects can neither lift a hardship nor shift it elsewhere. Commentators treat the second ayah as the practical edge of the first, since the ranking of prophets shows that even the highest creatures hold their standing as a gift.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch answering objections to the messenger's status. The commentators note that opponents questioned why this man had been chosen, and the reply widens the frame: prophets have always been given different measures, and one of them received a book of psalms. The challenge that follows was directed at a city whose shrines were its livelihood and its inheritance.

keyTerms.note: From a root for inscribing on stone or hide, so the emphasis falls on writing rather than recitation. It names the book given to David and appears in the Quran only in connection with him and his psalms.

The verb for pulling a covering off something. Applied to hardship it pictures relief as the lifting of a weight that was laid on, not the granting of something new, which is how the Quran usually frames rescue.
The word for moving a thing from one place to another. Paired with removal it closes the second escape route: whatever is invoked can neither end the trouble nor pass it along to somebody else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hardship in Mecca had recognisable faces. Drought that emptied wells, a caravan lost on the Syrian road, a fever that took a child in a night. When those arrived people went to the shrines with offerings, because that was what the shrines were for. The challenge in this ayah lands on ordinary practice rather than on theory, naming the exact moment when a family would have been standing before an image asking for the weight to lift.
studies.didYouKnow: The name for the scripture given to David occurs three times in the Quran, and two of them place it in his hands directly, inside lists of what was revealed to earlier prophets. The third occurrence carries the definite article and quotes a line from that book, saying the earth will be inherited by God's righteous servants.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ranking of prophets is stated without explanation, which quietly removes the argument that the latest messenger cannot be genuine because he lacks some feature an earlier one had. Distribution belongs to the giver. The challenge that follows rests on the same logic from the other end: anything that must be asked, and cannot answer, is receiving rather than giving. The passage tests claims about power by asking what they can actually do.

crossReferences.why: States the same ranking among messengers and lists some of the different gifts they received.
Quotes from the psalms given to David, the scripture named in the first ayah here.
Extends the same challenge, saying what is invoked besides God controls not even a date stone's husk.

studies.applyIt: Think about where your first call goes when something goes badly. Not what you believe about it, what you actually reach for in the first ten minutes: a person, a screen, a plan, a substance. Name it honestly, without judging yourself. Then next time, try putting one short direct request to God before you reach for it.

studies.title: Vying To Be Nearer
studies.meaning: The objects of invocation are described from their own side, and the description dismantles the practice without insulting anyone. Those being called are themselves seeking access, competing over who can come closest, hoping for mercy and fearing punishment. Commentators differ over exactly who is meant, some reading angels and righteous figures who were invoked without consenting to it, others reading spirits. All agree the argument is the same: whoever is still hoping and still afraid is in the queue, not at its head.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the challenge to call whatever is invoked besides God. The commentators report that some of what Mecca and its neighbours venerated had begun as reverence for beings the venerators considered close to God, rather than as an outright substitution. This ayah addresses that softer version, which is why it argues from the position of the intermediaries rather than denying their existence.

keyTerms.note: A noun for whatever brings you nearer to someone whose favour you want. It occurs only twice in the Quran, and in the other place believers are told to seek it, which is what these beings are doing here.
A comparative that makes the whole clause competitive: which of them is closer. Nearness is presented as something contested and worked for, not as a fixed rank anybody holds by nature.
A passive form from a root about wariness and taking precautions. It frames the punishment as something one takes measures about, rather than something one is simply terrified by.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in Arabia ran through intermediaries. To reach a chief you approached a man in his household; to enter another tribe's territory safely you sought the protection of somebody inside it who would vouch for you. The whole social world was built on brokered nearness, and the shrines were an extension of it. This ayah takes that familiar structure and points out that the brokers being paid are themselves petitioners further down the same line.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a means of approach appears only twice in the whole Quran. In the other passage believers are directly instructed to seek one. Read together, the two occurrences say that the search for nearness is right and that it is universal, and that beings the objectors were treating as the destination are in fact fellow travellers on the same road.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hope and fear are named together here as the condition of every created thing, including the highest. That places the believer and the greatest of creatures in the same posture, which is a levelling claim about creation rather than a warning about idols. It also explains why intercession appears in the Quran as something permitted rather than possessed: those who might intercede are described as still hoping for mercy themselves.

crossReferences.why: The only other place the word for a means of approach occurs, there as an instruction to believers.
Removes any independent authority from those invoked, and places intercession entirely under permission.
Describes honoured servants who never speak ahead of Him and act only on His word.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you route a request through someone: a manager, a friend of a friend, a person whose approval seems to gate the thing you want. Some of that is ordinary and fine. But pick one thing this week that you have been asking others about, and take it to God first, in your own words, before you take it to anyone else.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Inscribed In The Book
studies.meaning: Every settlement is placed under a term. Each will be destroyed or severely afflicted before the Day of Resurrection, and this is described as already written down. Commentators read the two outcomes as covering different cases rather than as alternatives for the same one, and they generally take the destruction to follow persistent wrongdoing rather than to fall at random. The force of the ayah is in its scope. No city is exempted, and the exception clause leaves nothing outside it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city confident of its own permanence. Mecca's standing rested on the sanctuary, the trade routes and an unbroken settlement that its people traced back generations. Caravans from Mecca passed the ruins of older Arabian towns twice a year on the roads north and south. The surah has already recalled two destructions in the history of the Children of Israel, so the theme is not introduced here for the first time.

keyTerms.note: Any gathered settlement, from a village to a city, and in the Quran usually standing for its people rather than its buildings. The word carries the sense of a population that has put down roots and expects to stay.

An active participle rather than a future verb, which in Arabic presents the act as settled and in hand. The grammar does not predict the end of the town so much as report an arrangement already made.
From a root for ruled lines of script. It suggests an orderly record rather than a note, and the Quran uses the same form elsewhere for a book of decree kept beyond human access.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian trade roads ran past abandoned towns. Ruined wells, cut rock dwellings and dead irrigation channels stood at intervals along the routes to Syria and Yemen, and merchants camped near them. Places that had once fed caravans were by then landmarks and nothing else. An audience that made the journey twice a year did not need the point explained; they had eaten dinner in the shadow of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact form used here for something written in lines occurs only twice in the Quran. Here it describes the recorded term of every town. In its other occurrence it describes the record in which the ties of kinship are set down. The same rare word covers the ending of cities and the binding of families.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the term of every settlement in a written record makes the fall of a civilisation a matter of appointment rather than accident, which changes how history can be read. It also removes a specific comfort. The ayah offers no category of city that is safe, so security cannot be located in walls, in trade, or in a sanctuary. What the Quran repeatedly locates it in instead is conduct, which is the one variable a community actually holds.

crossReferences.why: Gives every community an appointed term that cannot be brought forward or delayed.
Adds that no town is destroyed until a messenger has been sent to its main settlement first.
Sends the reader out to look at ruined towns and asks what the travellers' hearts learned there.

studies.applyIt: Find out what stood where you live before the current buildings did. A street name, an old map, a photograph, one question to someone older than you. Spend fifteen minutes on it this week. The point is not nostalgia. It is to feel, once and concretely, that the arrangement you treat as the permanent background arrived recently and is on a term.

studies.title: The Sign They Wounded
studies.meaning: A reason is given for something that looks like withholding. The demanded miracles are not sent because earlier peoples were given exactly that and denied it anyway, and the case named is Thamud, who received a she-camel as a sign made plain and then wronged her. The closing clause states the purpose of such signs in one word: they come to instil fear. Commentators note that a sign of that order is not a favour. It removes every excuse, and what follows a rejected sign has historically been severe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage answering demands for a spectacular proof. The classical sources report various things opponents asked for, and differ over the details, but agree that demands of this kind were repeatedly made and repeatedly declined. Thamud were a northern Arabian people whose rock-cut dwellings lay on the caravan road to Syria, so the example was not distant history for this audience.

keyTerms.note: An active form that can mean both plainly seen and causing others to see. Applied to the she-camel it says the sign was not obscure, which is what makes the response to it damning rather than understandable.

The verb for putting something out of its rightful place. The object here is the sign itself, so the crime is described as an injury done to the creature and to the meaning it carried at the same time.

A verbal noun naming the purpose rather than the effect. It occurs only here in the Quran and it reframes miracles: their function is to make a people careful, not to satisfy curiosity or settle a debate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A she-camel in milk was the most valuable animal a family could own, and one set aside with its own share of the water was a visible standing cost to everybody around it. Wells in northern Arabia were rationed by turns, and giving a whole day's turn to a single animal touched every household's herd. The sign was not an abstraction; it sat in the middle of the town's water rota where nobody could ignore it.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare word describing the she-camel as a sign made plain occurs three times in the Quran, and two of those are in this surah. Earlier it describes daylight itself, the sign of the day made visible so people can see by it. The same term covers an ordinary morning and a miracle, which quietly narrows the distance between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah explains a divine restraint in terms of mercy rather than inability. Sending an undeniable sign to people who will deny it anyway raises the cost of their refusal, so withholding it is a form of forbearance. That reverses the usual complaint. A generation not given a miracle is not being neglected; it is being left with room to move that earlier peoples spent. It also fixes the purpose of signs as reverence, not entertainment.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand by saying that even a requested sign would not have produced belief.
Tells the story of Thamud and the she-camel at length, including how the sign was destroyed.
Names the she-camel explicitly as a test sent to them, and counsels waiting and patience.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you asked for a clear sign about a decision. Now ask what you did with the last one you got, the small confirmation you noticed and then talked yourself out of. Write that one down tonight. Most of us are not short of signs. We are short of the willingness to be bound by them once they arrive.

studies.title: The Vision And The Tree
studies.meaning: A reassurance is recalled first: the Lord has encompassed the people, so they are surrounded and the messenger is not exposed. Then two things are named as a test. The vision he was shown, which most commentators connect with the Night Journey reported at the opening of this surah, and a tree the Quran calls cursed, generally identified with the tree of bitter fruit described in the descriptions of the Fire. Both were repeated in Mecca and both were used as grounds for ridicule, so what was given as evidence functioned as a sorting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical reports say the account of the night journey given by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was met with open disbelief when it was told in the city, and that some who had accepted the message turned back over it while others accepted it without hesitation. The commentators differ over whether the vision here was seen waking or in sleep, most holding the former.

keyTerms.note: The verb for enclosing something on every side, used of a wall around a garden. It carries both senses at once here, complete knowledge of people and complete containment of what they are able to do.
Originally the assaying of gold in fire to see what is genuinely in it. The word does not mean a trap. It means an event that reveals what was already there, which is how the passage uses it.
From a root for water rising past its banks. It pictures transgression as a flood exceeding a limit rather than as a decision, which fits a response that grew each time a warning arrived.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that a claim made in the morning was known across the city by evening. Trade to Jerusalem took a caravan roughly a month each way, and the men in the audience had walked that road and could price it. A report of a journey there and back in a night was therefore not vague to them; it collided with a distance they had personally measured in weeks of thirst and hired camels.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the definite word for the vision in only three places. In one, Abraham is told he has fulfilled the vision he was shown of his son. In another, the Prophet's vision of entering the Sacred Mosque in safety is confirmed as true. Here, the third, the vision is named a test for the people who heard about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something uncomfortable about evidence. Something given as a genuine sign can harden the very people it reaches, and the ayah accepts this as part of the design rather than treating it as a failure. Testing is presented as revealing rather than manufacturing: the mockery was already latent and the vision brought it out. Set beside the opening reassurance, the message is that being encompassed is protection for the messenger, not a guarantee of agreement from anyone.

crossReferences.why: Opens this surah with the journey by night that most commentators connect with the vision named here.
Describes the tree of the Fire that the classical commentators identify with the cursed tree.
States plainly that a detail of the Fire was made a test, and who it sorted.

studies.applyIt: Think of a claim about faith that you find hardest to say out loud to people who do not share it. Do not argue it with anyone this week. Just notice what happens in you when it comes up: the wish to soften it, to change the subject, to add a qualifier. That reaction is worth knowing about before you decide anything about it.

studies.title: Shall I Bow To Clay
studies.meaning: The surah turns from arguing with the objectors to the first refusal of all. The command is given, the angels comply, and one refuses with a question rather than a denial. His objection is entirely about material: he will not bow to something made of mud. Commentators note that the reasoning is a comparison, and that comparison is exactly what the command had bypassed. Nothing had been said about what Adam was made of. The honour was conferred, and the refusal answers the honour by grading the substance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Placing this scene here connects the surah's argument to its opening, since what the objectors refuse to grant a man from among themselves is what was refused at the beginning of the human story. The commentators treat this account as a recurring reference point across the Meccan surahs, told each time with a different emphasis rather than as a new report.

keyTerms.note: The word covers lowering oneself before someone in acknowledgement as well as prostration in worship. The classical commentators read the command here in the first sense, as an act of honouring done at God's instruction.

Earth mixed with water, the state before it is fired or dried. The Quran uses several words for the human origin at different stages, and this one names the most workable and least impressive of them.

The interrogative particle turns a command into an incredulous question. Arabic grammarians read this form as rejection expressed through astonishment, which is a refusal that presents itself as reasoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clay was the cheap material of that world. Ovens, water jars, storage pits and the flat roofs of houses were made from mud mixed and left in the sun, and it cracked, softened in rain and had to be patched every season. Rank in Mecca was traced through lineage, and a family's worth was argued from ancestry. An objection based on what somebody was made from would have sounded entirely familiar in that city.
studies.didYouKnow: The prostration before Adam is recounted seven times across the Quran, and the refusal is never given the same wording twice. In some tellings the reason is stated as fire against clay. Here no comparison of substances is completed; only the lower material is named, and the sentence stops there, leaving the implied claim about himself unspoken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The scene locates the first sin in a comparison rather than in an appetite. Nothing is wanted here and nothing is taken; a ranking is asserted, and the refusal follows from it. That makes the passage a study of pride specifically, and it explains why the Quran treats pride as the root failure rather than as one fault among many. The honour given to the human being is also established as conferred, not earned, which is why arguing from material misses it entirely.

crossReferences.why: Gives the refusal with the comparison completed: created from fire, against one made from clay.
Adds that the refusal was arrogance, and names what had been shaped with God's own hands.
States the honouring of Adam's children directly, a few ayat after this refusal of it.

studies.applyIt: Catch the next time you dismiss what someone says because of who they are: younger than you, less qualified, from the wrong department, a relative you have already categorised. Do not argue with yourself about it. Just take the thing they actually said, separate it from them, and give it thirty seconds of honest weight before you answer.

studies.title: A Reprieve And A Vow
studies.meaning: The refusal becomes a proposal. Given time until the Day of Resurrection, he undertakes to take the descendants of this honoured creature under his control, and he adds a limit himself: except a few. The reply grants the request without negotiating it and states the outcome in advance. Commentators note that the exception is conceded by the one making the boast, so the reach of the project is bounded by its own author before anyone contests it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been describing people who heard the recitation and refused it, and this scene supplies the wider frame those refusals sit inside. The classical commentators treat the exchange as belonging to the beginning of the human story rather than to any event of the Prophet's lifetime, recalled here because the surah is about what human beings do with an honour they have been given.

keyTerms.gloss: I will bridle, lead by rein
keyTerms.note: A verb from the word for the palate or the underside of the jaw, used of putting a rope in an animal's mouth to lead it. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it pictures direction rather than force.
The verb for postponing something already due, not for granting a new term. The request is therefore for delay of a sentence, which is why the reply reads as permission rather than as a gift.

A passive form from a root about completeness and paying in full, used in commerce for a debt settled without shortfall. It occurs only here, and it turns the recompense into a transaction discharged exactly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every household in Mecca knew the mouth rope. A camel is not driven but led, by a cord attached at the jaw, and a trained animal follows without resistance because it has stopped considering another direction. Caravan drivers walked ahead and the line came after them for weeks. The image in this vow is not capture and not violence. It is an animal walking willingly behind someone it has learned to follow.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words in these two ayat occur nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for leading by the jaw rope, and the adjective describing the recompense as paid in full. A single exchange of four sentences therefore carries two terms found in no other passage, one for the method and one for the settlement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reprieve raises a real difficulty and the passage does not soften it. Permission is granted, and yet the outcome is stated in the same breath, so nothing is left uncertain about where the arrangement ends. The exchange also defines the method precisely. What is proposed is guidance in the wrong direction, not compulsion, which is why the Quran elsewhere gives the tempter no authority and leaves responsibility with whoever followed.

crossReferences.why: Records the same figure admitting at the end that he only called, and they answered him.
Gives the parallel exchange with the reprieve granted and the same exception over sincere servants.
States the vow again with the exception named directly as God's sincere servants among them.

studies.applyIt: Think about what leads you rather than what pushes you: the app you open without deciding to, the route you drive on autopilot, the tone you fall into with one particular person. Pick the smallest of them and interrupt it once today. Not permanently. Just once, so you can feel the difference between being led and choosing.

studies.title: You Have No Authority
studies.meaning: The permission is spelled out in military language: unsettle them with your voice, bring cavalry and infantry against them, become a partner in their wealth and their children, and make them promises. Then the Quran breaks in to say what those promises are worth. The second ayah closes the passage from the other side. Over God's servants there is no authority at all, and the reader is left with a guarantor rather than a warning. Commentators read the whole permission as bounded by that single sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing the scene of the reprieve. The commentators do not report a particular occasion. They read the passage as addressed to a community that was small, watched and under real pressure in the city, which is why the description of assault is followed immediately by a statement that the assault has no purchase and by the naming of a guardian.

keyTerms.note: A verb for jolting someone out of a settled position so that they move before they think. Its root occurs only in this surah, three times, and it describes agitation rather than persuasion.

Horsemen, the most expensive and most feared element of any seventh-century force. Paired with those on foot it makes the picture a full mobilisation, which is exactly the scale the following ayah cancels.
From a root about being taken in by a surface. It names a promise that is not merely unkept but was never backed by anything, so the loss is discovered only when the promised thing is reached for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raid in Arabia began with noise. Riders came in at dawn shouting so the camp would scatter before it could form a line, because a settlement that panicked was taken by a much smaller force than one that stood. Horses were rare and expensive in the Hijaz and a family might own none, so cavalry meant a serious party with backing. The passage borrows the whole vocabulary of a raid and then removes its effect.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for startling someone out of their place occurs three times in the Quran, and all three are in this surah. Here it is the permission granted to the tempter. Later the opponents nearly do it to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), to drive him from the land, and later still Pharaoh intends it against Moses and his people.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a real threat beside a real limit and refuses to reduce either. Temptation is described with full military machinery, so it is not being minimised, and then it is denied any authority over God's servants, so it is not being feared either. The result is a specific kind of confidence: the pressure is genuine, the vulnerability is genuine, and neither of them decides the outcome. Reliance is offered as the answer rather than immunity.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit from the other direction, naming who the tempter does have authority over.
Has him disclaim any power at the end, saying he only called and they responded.
Uses the same word for an entrusted agent, there denied of the Prophet over his audience.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next urge that arrives with urgency attached, the one that says decide now. Whatever it is about, set a timer for ten minutes and do nothing until it rings. Most of what startles you into motion cannot survive ten quiet minutes, and you will learn something about which of your impulses actually belong to you.

studies.title: Ships Driven At Sea
studies.meaning: One sentence describes a whole economy and assigns it. Ships move across water so that people can go looking for what God has given, and the verb makes the movement something done for them rather than by them. The ayah then names the reason, and it is not power or design but mercy directed at these particular people. Commentators note the ordering. Trade is treated as a mercy before it is treated as a means, and the profit sought is called a portion of God's own bounty rather than a return on effort.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca lived on long-distance trade, and although the city itself sat inland, its merchants used the Red Sea ports and knew the sea route to Abyssinia well. Some of the earliest Muslims had crossed that water to seek refuge. The commentators report no specific occasion for this ayah and read it within a run of passages recalling ordinary benefits the audience received without noticing.

keyTerms.note: A verb for urging something forward slowly and steadily, the way a herd is moved. It occurs twice in the Quran, here of ships and elsewhere of clouds, so the same unhurried pushing carries both cargo and rain.

A word with the same form in singular and plural, so it can mean one vessel or a whole fleet without changing shape. The root also gives the word for an orbit, joining both to the idea of a rounded course.

From a root meaning what is left over beyond need. Applied to God it names giving that exceeds any claim, which is why earnings sought at sea are described as sought from Him rather than from the voyage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Red Sea was feared and used. Its coral shoals tore hulls, the wind reversed with the season, and vessels were sewn together with coconut cord rather than nailed, because iron was scarce and the joints had to flex. Crews hugged the coast and anchored at night. Every load of grain, cloth or incense that reached the Hijaz by water had come through that, and the people who ate the grain rarely thought about the crossing.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for driving the ships along appears only one other time in the Quran, where God is described as driving the clouds until they gather and the rain comes out from between them. The same gentle pushing carries a merchant's cargo across water and carries the water itself across the sky.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does something quiet to the idea of earning. It grants the whole enterprise, the voyage, the search and the profit, and then places the moving of the vessel outside the merchant's hands. Nothing is taken from human effort; the frame around it is changed. Mercy is also stated as the cause rather than the consequence, so the sea route exists because of an attitude God holds toward these people, not because they proved worthy of it.

crossReferences.why: The only other use of this verb, there of clouds driven until rain comes from their folds.
Says the sea was made subject so ships may run through it and bounty be sought there.
Lists ships running at sea for human benefit among the signs for people who reason.

studies.applyIt: Take one ordinary thing that reached you today from far away: the coffee, the phone in your hand, the fruit that is not in season here. Trace it backwards for two minutes. Who moved it, across what, at what risk. Then say a short thanks that names the thing specifically rather than thanking God for everything at once.

studies.title: When The Sea Turns
studies.meaning: A sequence is described rather than a doctrine. Harm reaches you on the water and everything else you call on goes missing, leaving only Him; He brings you to land, and you turn away. The closing clause generalises it as a human characteristic rather than a fault of one group. Commentators observe that the ayah does not accuse anyone of insincerity at sea. The appeal there was real. What it records is how quickly the ground of that appeal is forgotten once the danger is behind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the ayah about ships and trade. The commentators do not attach a specific occasion. They read it as addressed to a mercantile audience who had made exactly this kind of vow on a crossing, and note that the same pattern is described elsewhere of people who called on God in a storm and returned to their old practice on shore.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for losing one's way, used here of the objects of invocation themselves. They do not refuse; they go missing, as though they had wandered off, which is a quieter dismissal than any denial.
Literally to present your side to something rather than your face. The word describes turning away without argument or announcement, which is exactly how the forgetting after rescue tends to happen.
An intensive form from a root meaning to cover something over. Ingratitude in Arabic is not the absence of thanks but the burying of a benefit, so the person has to put the rescue out of sight first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel in the region was seasonal and unforgiving. A crew caught by a shift in the wind could be driven onto reefs within an hour, and vows made in that hour were common enough that they had recognised forms. Merchants pledged animals, portions of cargo, and sometimes their whole profit. Ports on the Red Sea had shrines that lived off exactly those promises, collected from men who had reached shore and remembered.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this scene of a storm at sea in several places, and the pattern is the same each time: sincere appeal on the water, forgetting once ashore. In one of those passages the people are described as calling on God with religion made purely His, using the phrase the Quran usually reserves for the highest sincerity, and then returning immediately to what they had before.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats sincerity as something a person can genuinely have and genuinely lose, which is more troubling than a claim that the sailors were pretending. It also makes an argument about knowledge. Under pressure the human being reaches accurately, past every intermediary, straight to the one who can act. That instinct is presented as evidence about how people are actually made, and the turning away afterwards as the thing that needs explaining.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same storm, with religion made sincerely His, and the same association resumed on land.
Draws out the scene at length, including the vow made and broken after safe arrival.
Adds that after rescue people divide, some keeping to moderation and others not.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time something frightening resolved well: a scan, a call, a near miss on the road. Try to remember what you promised in the middle of it. Most people find they cannot. Write down one small thing you would want to have promised, and do that thing this week while nothing is wrong.

studies.title: Are You Secure On Land
studies.meaning: The argument follows the rescued travellers onto the shore and takes their safety apart. The place they thought they had reached can open under them, or the sky above it can send a storm of stones, and there would be nobody to answer for them. Commentators note the precision of the wording: a stretch of the coast, not the whole earth, so the threat is local and ordinary rather than apocalyptic. The point is not that land is dangerous. It is that the sense of arrival was never a change in exposure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing directly from the description of vows made at sea and abandoned on land. The commentators report no particular occasion. They read the two questions that follow as pressing an audience that had drawn a line between danger and safety in the wrong place, and note that both dangers named were familiar to anyone who had travelled the Arabian roads.

keyTerms.note: From the root that also gives the words for faith and for trust. The question therefore asks where the audience has placed its sense of safety, using the same vocabulary the Quran uses for belief itself.
The verb for ground giving way and taking what stood on it downward. It is used of a specific event rather than of general ruin, so the picture is a collapse in one place, not the end of everything.

Wind carrying gravel and pebbles hard enough to strip a caravan. The word occurs four times in the Quran, in each case for a punishment delivered by something ordinary in the landscape rather than by anything unfamiliar.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both dangers were seen, not imagined. The volcanic country around Medina is scattered with collapsed lava tubes where the crust drops without warning, and travellers avoided certain stretches for that reason. Sandstorms on the northern route stripped paint from a saddle and buried the track entirely, and a party caught in one lay flat beside their animals and waited. Reaching shore or reaching a road changed which risk you faced, not whether you faced one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for an entrusted guardian occurs five times in this surah, more often than in any other. It moves between roles as it goes: forbidden to the Children of Israel to seek besides God, denied of the Prophet over his audience, affirmed of the Lord as sufficient, and twice denied here to people looking for someone to answer for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage relocates security rather than removing it. Nothing here says the world is arbitrary or that harm falls at random; what it says is that the ground itself is held, and the sense of having arrived somewhere safe is a description of feeling rather than of fact. That is not an argument for anxiety. It is an argument that the reliance offered at sea was never meant to be temporary, and that the shore is the same arrangement wearing a calmer face.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same pair of questions in the same order, about the earth swallowing and a stone-laden wind.
Shows the earth actually opening on a man whose wealth had convinced him he was secure.
Puts the same question to schemers, adding that seizure may come while they go about ordinarily.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing that makes you feel safe: a balance in an account, a job title, a person who is always there. Do not try to give it up. Just say plainly to yourself, once, that it is held rather than solid. Then notice whether the day feels different when the safety is on loan instead of owned.

studies.title: No One To Follow Up
studies.meaning: The second question sends the traveller back out. Having been delivered once, he could be returned to the water, met by a wind that snaps whatever it strikes, and drowned, and the ground given is his own ingratitude rather than any new offence. The closing word is the sharpest. Nobody would come after Us on your behalf to pursue the matter. Commentators read the pair of questions as closing both exits, since the first removed safety on land and this one removes the assumption that a rescue already granted cannot be revisited.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to merchants who crossed the Red Sea repeatedly rather than once. The commentators report no occasion for it and read it within the run of ayat about vows made in a storm. The point about a second crossing had force for that audience precisely because trade was seasonal: whoever came home in one season expected to sail again in the next.

keyTerms.note: From a root for breaking something with a loud crack, used of thunder and of a mast going. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it names the wind by the sound of what it destroys.

A word for a single turn or instance in a repeated series. It makes the second voyage an ordinary repetition rather than a new trial, which is why the question lands on people who assumed the danger was behind them.
Someone who follows up a debt or a killing on another's behalf until it is answered for. It occurs only here, and it borrows the vocabulary of tribal redress to say that no such advocate exists.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on the certainty that someone would follow up. A man killed on the road had kin who would pursue the matter for years, and that expectation was what kept travellers alive more than any weapon. To be without a pursuer was to be genuinely unprotected, which is why a stranger with no tribe sought a patron before doing anything else. The last word of this ayah removes exactly that guarantee.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this single ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the wind named for the sound of things snapping, and the term for a kinsman who pursues a claim on your behalf. One ayah about a sea crossing carries two words the rest of the Book never uses again, one at each end of the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes a point about how deliverance is understood. A rescue does not establish a precedent, and treating it as one turns a mercy into an entitlement, which is what the ingratitude in the previous ayah consisted of. The final word then closes the last available appeal. There is no higher court and no relative to raise the matter, which places the relationship with God outside every structure of leverage the audience knew.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same storm at length and describes the turning away that follows a safe landing.
Asks the same kind of question about the sky and earth, closing the exits above and below.
Says the ships could be stilled on the surface, or wrecked, and much still pardoned.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good outcome you have started treating as normal: your health, a marriage that held, work that came through. Say out loud once today that it was given rather than owed. It takes ten seconds and it is oddly difficult, which is the useful part. Notice which one you found hardest to say.

studies.title: We Honoured The Children Of Adam
studies.meaning: Four verbs, and the honour comes first. Human beings are dignified, carried on land and sea, provided with good things, and preferred over much of what was created. The commentators offer several grounds for the honouring: speech, reason, upright stature, the hand, the capacity to be addressed by God. Note the limit in the last clause, which says over many of those We created rather than over all, and the classical discussion turns on that word.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah arrives immediately after a passage about people who call on God at sea and forget Him on land, and just before a scene of the Day when every community is summoned. Placing an unqualified statement of human dignity between ingratitude and judgement is deliberate. The commentators report no specific occasion. The surah dates from the last Meccan years, when the community was small and despised.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for nobility and generosity. It describes conferring worth rather than recognising it, so the dignity is presented as given rather than earned or possessed by nature.
The verb for bearing a load. Applied to travel it credits the crossing itself to God rather than to the ship or the camel, which is a way of saying that mobility is also a gift.
A plural adjective used as a noun, covering food, and by extension whatever is clean and fit. The word marks quality rather than quantity, so the provision described is not simply abundance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land and sea were the two ways out of Arabia and both were dangerous. Caravans crossed months of desert with camels that could be lost to thirst or theft; ships from the Red Sea ports ran with the season and sank often enough that a merchant family expected losses. To be carried on both was not a figure of speech. It named the two arrangements on which every Meccan fortune depended.
studies.didYouKnow: The honour is given to the Children of Adam, not to believers, so it covers every human being without condition. Classical commentators drew the point out explicitly, and it has been cited for centuries in discussions of how the dead and the enemy are to be treated. Nothing in the ayah is made to depend on faith or conduct.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Human worth is stated as a fact about God's action rather than as a conclusion about human qualities. That places it beyond argument and beyond forfeiture: nothing a person does can make them not a child of Adam. The qualification in the final clause is equally deliberate. Preference over many, rather than over all, leaves the ranking open and keeps the honouring from becoming a claim of supremacy over creation.

crossReferences.why: The angels are told to bow before Adam, the first form the honouring takes.
States the same dignity in the shortest form: made in the best of moulds.
Draws the consequence: one life taken unjustly counts as all of humanity.

studies.applyIt: Look for the person today whose work makes your day possible and whom you would normally not see: the cleaner, the driver, the one restocking the shelf. Say something to them that is not about the task. The ayah does not make the honour conditional on anything, and treating it that way costs about eleven seconds.

studies.title: Called With Their Leader
studies.meaning: People are summoned in groups rather than as isolated individuals, each group named by something that stands at its head. Commentators differ over what that is: the prophet they followed, the record of their deeds, or the leader they took.
